# The Quadrennial Cycle: Four Generic Year-Directions, Individualized by Stage Objectives

**What it is** — Issurin frames multi-year planning around the four-year Olympic
cycle, triggered by post-Games analysis: "the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to
internalize positive experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based
on the findings, a new preparatory plan is worked out" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132).
He gives a worked example: the Russian national gymnastics team's quadrennial cycle,
subdivided into **eight half-year stages**, each with its own general objective (PDF p.
144, printed p. 133, cited to Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004): (1) enhancement of
sport-specific motor fitness; (2) acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and
their hybrids; (3) updating of competition combinations; (4) further increases in
sport-specific motor fitness; (5) enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable
performances; (6) increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance; (7)
final compilation of competition combinations, endurance for an entire program, and
selection of a duplicate Olympic squad; (8) modeling expected competitive conditions,
attaining high competitive reliability, and final selection of the Olympic team. Issurin
is explicit that this eight-stage division is sport-specific ("a matter of professional
competence" depending on conditions), and that "the division of the quadrennial cycle
into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).

For the four-annual-cycle version, Table 4.4 (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133; verified
against the page image) gives generic year-by-year directions, irrespective of sport:
**Year 1** — engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2**: further candidate selection
and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,
improved training quality; **Year 3**: attaining maximal training-workload level,
approving the Olympic-season annual cycle, determining individual performance
characteristics per team member; **Year 4**: stabilizing team make-up (usually with a
double Olympic squad), stabilizing workloads at the prior year's level, and approving
and stabilizing competitive behavior and performance. Issurin states the third and
fourth years "should be very similar since coaches simulate the annual pre-Olympic
training design one year before" the Games, though the pre-Olympic (fourth) year's
workload is "usually higher than the year before for various reasons," including
"greater motivation, better conditions for training and restoration, greater budgets"
(PDF p. 146, printed p. 135).

**Why it works** — The author gives no controlled-comparison mechanism for why
this generic four-year sequence outperforms an alternative structure; it is presented as
observed common practice ("the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual
cycles is the most popular") rationalized post hoc by the logic of squad-building
(candidate selection and cohesion before workload escalation, workload escalation
before stabilization). **Inference:** the underlying logic parallels this library's existing
long-term athletic development material: building foundational capacity (team
identity, basic skill acquisition) before layering higher, more specific workloads, but
Issurin does not state that connection explicitly in this passage.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — College football has no
literal Olympic quadrennium, but the four-year (or five-year, with a redshirt) eligibility
window is a structurally similar bounded multi-year cycle with its own roster-cohort
logic: Year 1 (true freshman/transfer intake) mapping to Table 4.4's Year 1 emphasis on
candidate evaluation and cultural integration; Years 2-3 to skill/technical acquisition
and rising training-workload tolerance; a "walk year" (senior or draft-eligible year)
to Table 4.4's Year 4 emphasis on stabilized, individualized performance. The
gymnastics eight-stage example is a useful illustration that objective-setting per stage
should be concrete and sport-specific rather than generic, which is directly usable
guidance for building a position-group or class-cohort development plan.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** both the eight-stage
gymnastics example and the four-year Table 4.4 are drawn from Olympic individual/
team-technical sports with a single fixed quadrennial target and squad continuity
controlled by national-team selection, not from a college roster with annual signing
classes, transfer portal turnover, and no shared four-year entry cohort (a program's
"Year 1" and "Year 4" athletes are present simultaneously every season, unlike a
national team's cycle-wide cohort). The table's per-year directions are the author's own
applied synthesis of common practice, not a study with an outcome measure; no
evidence is given that following this sequence produces better long-term results than
an alternative one. The Table 4.4 vs Fig. 4.5 age-cohort content (older/experienced vs.
younger-athlete workload differentiation within this same quadrennial frame) is
treated separately in
[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].

**Example** — **Inference:** a position group's four-year development plan borrowing
Table 4.4's shape: Year 1 focused on evaluating and culturally onboarding new signees
and transfers; Year 2 on techno-tactical (scheme/position) skill acquisition and raising
training-load tolerance; Year 3 on maximizing training workload and identifying each
player's individual performance profile; Year 4 on stabilizing role, workload, and
game-performance consistency for players entering their final season or a likely draft
evaluation.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].

# Older, Experienced Athletes Enter a New Quadrennial Cycle Lighter and Climb Back Slower

**What it is** — Within the quadrennial frame, Issurin differentiates preparation for
"highly experienced top-level athletes" (who "have a remarkable advantage in terms of
basic and sport-specific knowledge, emotional control, stability of technical,
techno-tactical skills and competitive behavior," and are usually "high-authority
persons who positively affect social climate and team spirit") from younger athletes new
to the Olympic cycle (PDF p. 145, printed p. 134). The stated disadvantage of the older
group: they are "approaching their biological limits in regard to training responses,"
show "less reactivity to training stimuli," prefer habitual programs, need longer
transition periods, and, in the first annual cycle of a new quadrennial plan, train at
"a substantially lower total volume of exercises, about 15-20% less, than in the
previous Olympic year" (PDF p. 145, printed p. 134; text quote). Younger athletes new
to Olympic preparation show the opposite pattern: heightened motivation, often better
training conditions (more camps, more qualified partners), and a substantial workload
increase in year one relative to the prior year, continuing to rise at a diminishing rate
through years two and three.

**Verified against the page image (Fig. 4.5, PDF p. 145, printed p. 134):** the chart
plots "total workloads, referring units" across five time points (prior Olympic Games,
then Years I, II, III, and the next Olympic Games) for both groups. Younger athletes
rise steadily from about 7.4 at the prior Games to about 10.0 at the next Games.
Experienced athletes fall sharply from about 10 (at the prior Games, their own peak
taper year) to about 7 at Year I: **a drop of roughly 30%, not the "about 15-20%
less" the text states**, then climb through about 8.1, 8.6 to about 9.0 at the next
Games, ending below the younger group's 10.0. This is a text-vs-figure inconsistency
of the same kind found in the Chapter 3 review (Fig. 3.10's "69.3%" versus the plotted
value); it is recorded here rather than silently resolved. The qualitative pattern the text
describes, older athletes drop, then climb back more slowly than they descended,
finishing below younger athletes, matches the figure regardless of the exact percentage.

Table 4.5 (PDF p. 147, printed p. 136; verified against the page image) generalizes this
across the whole career, not just the first quadrennial year: **total training volume**
10-30% less than younger athletes ("older athletes train more conscientiously and
produce longer training residuals"); **annual cycle structure**: longer transition
period ("additional time for psychological and medical rehabilitation"); **organizational
forms**: higher share of individual (vs. group) training ("aged athletes need less
supervision, show more initiative and independence"); **restoration**: increased use of
restorative means ("older athletes recover slower and often suffer from previous
injuries"); **equipment**: more insistent, creative selection ("their own demands...
serious and consistent during their examination"); **individual progress**: "motor
potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively," i.e. "stabilization and
reduction of several functions are compensated for by higher efficiency of athletic
activity."

**Why it works** — The author gives no physiological mechanism for the biological
"approaching their limits" claim beyond naming it; the entry that follows in Table 4.5
attributes the compensating higher performance to behavioral factors (conscientiousness,
individualized training, restoration, equipment care) and to "higher efficiency of
athletic activity" rather than to any stated biological process. **Inference:** this
pairs naturally with this library's existing residual-training-effect material: a more
trained system plausibly needs a smaller absolute training dose to hold a given
adaptation, but Issurin does not make that specific connection in this passage.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college roster** — A fifth-year or
graduate-transfer player entering a new coaching cycle, offseason, or scheme after
several years in a program is a rough structural analogue to Issurin's "experienced
athlete entering a new quadrennial cycle": expect (and program for) a lower initial
training volume than a true freshman or new transfer, a longer individualized
restoration/return-to-training window, and a training emphasis on utilization and
technical/tactical efficiency over raw volume increases, consistent with Table 4.5's
"motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** this is Issurin's own applied
generalization about elite, Olympic-cycle, mostly-individual-sport athletes typically in
their late 20s to 30s; it is not derived from a controlled or longitudinal study with
football-specific data, and "older" in this context (returning multi-Olympiad veterans)
does not map cleanly onto a 22-23-year-old college fifth-year player, whose biological
age is nowhere near the "biological limits" the text describes for career-long elite
athletes. The 15-20%/10-30% figures are the author's own stated bands, not derived
from a cited dataset in this passage, and (per the figure check above) the book's own
chart does not match its own 15-20% claim for the first-year drop.

**Example** — **Inference:** a fifth-year offensive lineman returning after a coaching
staff or scheme change is deliberately started at a lower total training-volume target
than the incoming freshman class, with a longer individualized ramp and an emphasis
on technical efficiency (leverage, hand placement, pass-set footwork) rather than
chasing the volume numbers of his own earlier seasons, consistent with the
"motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively" framing.

# Klementiev: Training Volume Fell for 19 Years While Podium Results Kept Coming

**What it is** — A single-athlete, 19-year longitudinal case: Ivan Klementiev, USSR
then Latvian Olympic canoeist, competed across four Olympic cycles, earning one gold
and two silver Olympic medals and seven World Championship golds (PDF p. 148,
printed p. 137). His total annual paddling volume was tracked by age (Figure 4.6, PDF
p. 149, printed p. 138; **verified against the page image**: the chart's peak at age 21,
roughly 4,900 km, matches the text's "maximal training volume was attained at age 21
when he trained with the USSR national squad"; volume then oscillates with periodic
late-quadrennial upticks but trends down through the following years, with the lowest
point at age 37, about 1,500 km). Issurin quantifies the decline by quadrennial-cycle
average, relative to the first cycle as 100%: **ages 21-24 = 100%; ages 25-28 = 88.2%;
ages 29-32 = 77.4%; ages 33-36 = 61%** (PDF p. 148, printed p. 137; text quote).
Transition periods lengthened over the same span, "from one to three months during
his career." Despite the steady volume decline, "after age 30 [he] won four gold medals
at the World Championships and two Olympic silver medals" (PDF p. 149, printed p.
138). Issurin's own conclusion: "workload reduction was effectively compensated for
by a higher quality of training," which he associates with the athlete's own account
(Klementiev, 1994) of "better preparation exploiting Block Periodization, a more
conscious and effective selection of exercises, avoidance of non-compatible workload
combinations, constant attention to restoration, and the use of a logical program of
competition." One deviation in the record is flagged as non-methodological: at age 24
(1984), "because of political, not methodological circumstances," Klementiev raced a
substitute regatta of socialist countries rather than the Los Angeles Olympics, cutting
that season short by a month (Figure 4.6 caption, PDF p. 149, printed p. 138).

**Why it works** — The author's own causal claim ("workload reduction was
effectively compensated for by a higher quality of training") is stated, not
demonstrated: no comparison group, no measured "training quality" variable, and no
separation of the Block Periodization approach from the other listed factors (exercise
selection, compatibility management, restoration, competition-program logic) or from
simple accumulated technical/tactical experience. **The author gives no mechanism**
connecting reduced kilometers specifically to Block Periodization as opposed to any
other explanation for late-career success, including selection effects (an athlete who
stays competitive to age 36 across four Olympiads is, by construction, one of the rare
athletes for whom this pattern worked).

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — Useful as a
citable, named-athlete illustration that declining training volume is not, by itself,
evidence of declining performance capacity in an experienced athlete, and that
tracking quality/specificity of training rather than raw volume may be the more
relevant monitoring question for a veteran player. Pairs directly with
[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]]'s Table
4.5 claim that "motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is an n = 1, uncontrolled,
retrospective case with no comparison athlete who trained at a constant or rising
volume across the same span; it cannot separate the effect of reduced volume, Block
Periodization specifically, accumulated technical mastery, opponent turnover, or
survivorship (only athletes who remained competitive despite aging appear in this kind
of retrospective record; athletes for whom volume reduction did not work are absent
from it by definition). It is also a single elite paddler in an individual, cyclic-endurance
Olympic sport with a fixed quadrennial target; nothing here generalizes to a college
football roster's age range (18-23), position-specific demands, or annual (not
quadrennial) competitive cycle. Do not cite this case as evidence that reducing training
volume improves or preserves performance in general.

**Example** — **Inference:** when a program has a small number of veteran players
whose measured training volumes are trending down year over year, Klementiev's case
is a reason to check training quality, technical execution, and competition-readiness
markers before treating the volume decline itself as a red flag, rather than a license to
assume volume reduction is automatically beneficial.

**Related** — [[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
[[case-study--armstrong-physiological-utilization-over-a-doping-era-career]].

# Armstrong's Seven-Point Physiology Case: Read Only With the Doping Context the 2008 Book Does Not Give

**Historical context absent from the source, stated first because it governs how the
rest of this entry should be read:** this book was published in 2008. Lance Armstrong
was stripped of all seven Tour de France titles (1999-2005) by the USADA "Reasoned
Decision" in 2012, following a finding of systematic doping (EPO, blood transfusions,
testosterone, corticosteroids) across the span this case study covers. That finding is not
in this book and could not have been reflected in it. This is stated as historical fact, not
as this entry-writer's opinion or as Eric's judgment; it is not labeled "Inference" because
it is not a reasoned inference from the text but an external, independently documented
fact about the case's subject. It means the physiological changes below cannot be read
as evidence of natural, doping-free long-term adaptation, and the case should not be
cited in that way.

**What it is** — Issurin presents cyclist Lance Armstrong as a case study in long-term
physiological change, based on Coyle (2005), a published laboratory case-report of
serial testing from age 21 to 28 (PDF p. 150, printed p. 139; text quote): "From ages 21
to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body composition, maximal
oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical efficiency of pedaling." At age 24
he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and underwent surgery and a two-year course
of treatment including chemotherapy; from ages 27-32 he won the Tour de France six
times (per the book's count at time of writing). Over the seven-year span, body weight
rose slightly (+0.8 kg) while lean body weight rose more (+1.1 kg). **Verified against
the page image (Figure 4.7, PDF p. 151, printed p. 140):** the chart is two twin-axis
panels across nine unevenly spaced age points (21.1, 21.4, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28), a
hollow-star marker flagging the "medical treatment including chemotherapy" period
around age 24-25. Top panel: Heart Rate (left axis, 196-208 beats/min) and VO2max
(right axis, 60-85 ml/kg/min); bottom panel: mechanical efficiency (right axis,
20-23.5%) and power output at a VO2 of 5 L/min (left axis, 370-420 W), the latter two
rising together and roughly linearly across all nine points. The two top-panel series are
not unambiguously distinguishable from the rendered image alone (their in-panel labels
sit near line peaks without a clear leader-line to one series), so the values below are
taken from the book's stated text, not read independently off the chart: **maximum
heart rate decreased by 6 beats/min** over the seven years; **VO2max "reached peak
value at age 23, declined after medical treatment and did not reach the highest level
until age 28"**; **mechanical efficiency increased by 8.8%**; **power output at 5 L/min
VO2 increased by 18%**. The book flags that Armstrong's final VO2max, 71 ml/kg/min,
is "inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 ml/kg/min
(Padilla et al., 2000)," and speculates this partly reflects body-weight reduction before

14	
15	# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions
16	
17	**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual
18	program (Table 4.2, PDF p. 138, printed p. 127), illustrated stepwise in Figures 4.1-4.4
19	(PDF pp. 139-141, printed pp. 128-130; verified against the page images): (1) determine
20	the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
21	regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
22	("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
23	several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
24	the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
25	(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
26	medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
27	calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
28	lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
29	previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
30	a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
31	4.1-4.4 show competitions plotted on four levels (Level A = the single targeted event;
32	Levels B-D = mandatory events of descending importance: national championship,
33	national cup, regional trials, winter cup), against a month-by-month grid that only
34	fills in stages/periods, meso/microcycles and training camps in the later figures as each
35	step is completed. The **optimal design places important competitions at the end of a
36	training stage** (Fig. 4.2 caption, PDF p. 139, printed p. 128). The plan is not
37	considered final at step 9: "it must first be reviewed by the administration, colleagues
38	and athletes and with repeated analysis, will lead to corrections" (PDF p. 141, printed
39	p. 130) before it "receives the final version status that is used for realization."
40	
41	Layered on this procedure is a seasonal content trend (Table 4.3, PDF p. 142, printed p.
42	131; verified against the page image): early season favors continuous/uniform/
43	alternating methods in the accumulation mesocycle and a wide range of fitness
44	exercises, more individual workouts, and general restorative means (stretching,
45	relaxation, low-intensity aerobics); mid-season narrows toward interval methods, a
46	restricted exercise range, and adds physiotherapy/massage/mental training/nutritional
47	supplements; late season is "strictly programmed interval exercises" in both
48	accumulation and transmutation mesocycles, mostly specialized exercises, strictly
49	programmed workouts, and the "most effective individually selected restorative
50	means." The general rule: "training stages within the annual cycle should be similar
51	but not identical," with mid- and especially late-season stages "more rigorous, more
52	strictly programmed and better managed" (PDF p. 142, printed p. 131).
53	
54	Issurin also assigns competition an explicit developmental role even early in the
55	season, for three stated reasons (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132): it completes each
56	training stage as "a compulsory component of the training program"; it "breaks the
57	usual routine and brings out the very important element of athlete spirit"; and it
58	"provides athletes with extraordinary training stimuli that can not be obtained from
59	regular workloads." The competitive program itself should be diversified early season,
60	narrowed toward event-specific standards mid-season, and strictly event-specific late
61	season.
62	
63	**Why it works** — The author's own stated rationale for reserving the most rigorous,
64	best-managed workloads for the pre-competition stages is two-part (PDF p. 142,
65	printed p. 131): physiologically, it "gives the benefit of higher training responses
66	prior to the most important events"; psychologically, "it heightens the athletes'
67	self-confidence as they know that they have additional reserves during the most
68	stressful phase of their preparation." No further mechanism is given for why the
69	nine-step sequence itself (as opposed to some other ordering) produces a better plan
70	than ad hoc planning; the author states only that "coaches put together annual
71	programs based on their own experience, knowledge and common sense" and that
72	Block Periodization "implies specific demands to planning" without benchmarking the
73	sequence against an alternative (PDF p. 138, printed p. 127).
74	
75	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — The Level
76	A/B/C/D competition tiers map reasonably well onto a football master calendar: Level
77	A as the postseason target (playoff/bowl window), Level B as rivalry or
78	conference-championship-implication games, Level C/D as the rest of the regular-season
79	slate. Step 1 (fix the target and mandatory events) and step 5 (plan camps, including
80	fall camp) are directly usable planning anchors for Applied Performance's annual
81	calendar-building work with the sport coaching staff. The step-7/8 "integrative
82	workload characteristics per month, compared with previous years" is a concrete,
83	citable structure for what a season-over-season GPS/load report should track, distinct
84	from (and a possible template for) the currently undocumented "standardized
85	weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting" gap named in `method-baseline.md` (Data,
86	technology and reporting section, line 159).
87	
88	**When NOT to apply** — This is Issurin's own applied planning template for an
89	individual/dual-sport Olympic calendar with a single clearly ranked target competition
90	determined well in advance; it is not derived from any comparative study of planning
91	methods (no control condition, no outcome data for the sequence itself). **Inference,
92	population caveat:** college football's postseason destination (which bowl, or which
93	playoff round) is not known when the annual plan is first built, which weakens step 1's
94	premise that the target competition can be fixed at the top of the sequence the way an
95	Olympic Trials date or a World Championship date can be; the plan has to accommodate
96	a moving Level-A target rather than a scheduled one. The "optimal design places
97	important competitions at the end of a training stage" (Fig. 4.2) also assumes the coach
98	controls stage boundaries around the competition calendar; in football the
99	competition calendar (one game almost every week, in season) is closer to Issurin's
100	"competitive microcycle" pattern described elsewhere in this book than to a plan with
101	discrete preparation stages ending in isolated target events.
102	
103	**Example** — **Inference:** using the nine-step sequence as a working checklist for a
104	Baylor football annual calendar: fix the bowl/playoff-window target and the
105	conference-championship-implication games (step 1); block out fall camp, the
106	regular-season in-season maintenance stage, and the bowl-prep stage (step 2-3); slot
107	non-conference "trial" games and any scrimmages (step 4); place fall camp and any
108	summer training windows (step 5); align the pre-participation physical and preseason
109	testing battery to early season (step 6); build a month-by-month GPS/load-volume
110	summary (step 7-8) and review it against the prior season before finalizing (step 9).
111	
112	**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]],
113	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
114	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
115	[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]].

129	
130	# The Quadrennial Cycle: Four Generic Year-Directions, Individualized by Stage Objectives
131	
132	**What it is** — Issurin frames multi-year planning around the four-year Olympic
133	cycle, triggered by post-Games analysis: "the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to
134	internalize positive experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based
135	on the findings, a new preparatory plan is worked out" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132).
136	He gives a worked example: the Russian national gymnastics team's quadrennial cycle,
137	subdivided into **eight half-year stages**, each with its own general objective (PDF p.
138	144, printed p. 133, cited to Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004): (1) enhancement of
139	sport-specific motor fitness; (2) acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and
140	their hybrids; (3) updating of competition combinations; (4) further increases in
141	sport-specific motor fitness; (5) enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable
142	performances; (6) increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance; (7)
143	final compilation of competition combinations, endurance for an entire program, and
144	selection of a duplicate Olympic squad; (8) modeling expected competitive conditions,
145	attaining high competitive reliability, and final selection of the Olympic team. Issurin
146	is explicit that this eight-stage division is sport-specific ("a matter of professional
147	competence" depending on conditions), and that "the division of the quadrennial cycle
148	into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).
149	
150	For the four-annual-cycle version, Table 4.4 (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133; verified
151	against the page image) gives generic year-by-year directions, irrespective of sport:
152	**Year 1** — engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
153	staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
154	repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2**: further candidate selection
155	and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,
156	improved training quality; **Year 3**: attaining maximal training-workload level,
157	approving the Olympic-season annual cycle, determining individual performance
158	characteristics per team member; **Year 4**: stabilizing team make-up (usually with a
159	double Olympic squad), stabilizing workloads at the prior year's level, and approving
160	and stabilizing competitive behavior and performance. Issurin states the third and
161	fourth years "should be very similar since coaches simulate the annual pre-Olympic
162	training design one year before" the Games, though the pre-Olympic (fourth) year's
163	workload is "usually higher than the year before for various reasons," including
164	"greater motivation, better conditions for training and restoration, greater budgets"
165	(PDF p. 146, printed p. 135).
166	
167	**Why it works** — The author gives no controlled-comparison mechanism for why
168	this generic four-year sequence outperforms an alternative structure; it is presented as
169	observed common practice ("the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual
170	cycles is the most popular") rationalized post hoc by the logic of squad-building
171	(candidate selection and cohesion before workload escalation, workload escalation
172	before stabilization). **Inference:** the underlying logic parallels this library's existing
173	long-term athletic development material: building foundational capacity (team
174	identity, basic skill acquisition) before layering higher, more specific workloads, but
175	Issurin does not state that connection explicitly in this passage.
176	
177	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — College football has no
178	literal Olympic quadrennium, but the four-year (or five-year, with a redshirt) eligibility
179	window is a structurally similar bounded multi-year cycle with its own roster-cohort
180	logic: Year 1 (true freshman/transfer intake) mapping to Table 4.4's Year 1 emphasis on
181	candidate evaluation and cultural integration; Years 2-3 to skill/technical acquisition
182	and rising training-workload tolerance; a "walk year" (senior or draft-eligible year)
183	to Table 4.4's Year 4 emphasis on stabilized, individualized performance. The
184	gymnastics eight-stage example is a useful illustration that objective-setting per stage
185	should be concrete and sport-specific rather than generic, which is directly usable
186	guidance for building a position-group or class-cohort development plan.
187	
188	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** both the eight-stage
189	gymnastics example and the four-year Table 4.4 are drawn from Olympic individual/
190	team-technical sports with a single fixed quadrennial target and squad continuity
191	controlled by national-team selection, not from a college roster with annual signing
192	classes, transfer portal turnover, and no shared four-year entry cohort (a program's
193	"Year 1" and "Year 4" athletes are present simultaneously every season, unlike a
194	national team's cycle-wide cohort). The table's per-year directions are the author's own
195	applied synthesis of common practice, not a study with an outcome measure; no
196	evidence is given that following this sequence produces better long-term results than
197	an alternative one. The Table 4.4 vs Fig. 4.5 age-cohort content (older/experienced vs.
198	younger-athlete workload differentiation within this same quadrennial frame) is
199	treated separately in
200	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
201	
202	**Example** — **Inference:** a position group's four-year development plan borrowing
203	Table 4.4's shape: Year 1 focused on evaluating and culturally onboarding new signees
204	and transfers; Year 2 on techno-tactical (scheme/position) skill acquisition and raising
205	training-load tolerance; Year 3 on maximizing training workload and identifying each
206	player's individual performance profile; Year 4 on stabilizing role, workload, and
207	game-performance consistency for players entering their final season or a likely draft
208	evaluation.
209	
210	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
211	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
212	[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].

227	# Older, Experienced Athletes Enter a New Quadrennial Cycle Lighter and Climb Back Slower
228	
229	**What it is** — Within the quadrennial frame, Issurin differentiates preparation for
230	"highly experienced top-level athletes" (who "have a remarkable advantage in terms of
231	basic and sport-specific knowledge, emotional control, stability of technical,
232	techno-tactical skills and competitive behavior," and are usually "high-authority
233	persons who positively affect social climate and team spirit") from younger athletes new
234	to the Olympic cycle (PDF p. 145, printed p. 134). The stated disadvantage of the older
235	group: they are "approaching their biological limits in regard to training responses,"
236	show "less reactivity to training stimuli," prefer habitual programs, need longer
237	transition periods, and, in the first annual cycle of a new quadrennial plan, train at
238	"a substantially lower total volume of exercises, about 15-20% less, than in the
239	previous Olympic year" (PDF p. 145, printed p. 134; text quote). Younger athletes new
240	to Olympic preparation show the opposite pattern: heightened motivation, often better
241	training conditions (more camps, more qualified partners), and a substantial workload
242	increase in year one relative to the prior year, continuing to rise at a diminishing rate
243	through years two and three.
244	
245	**Verified against the page image (Fig. 4.5, PDF p. 145, printed p. 134):** the chart
246	plots "total workloads, referring units" across five time points (prior Olympic Games,
247	then Years I, II, III, and the next Olympic Games) for both groups. Younger athletes
248	rise steadily from about 7.4 at the prior Games to about 10.0 at the next Games.
249	Experienced athletes fall sharply from about 10 (at the prior Games, their own peak
250	taper year) to about 7 at Year I: **a drop of roughly 30%, not the "about 15-20%
251	less" the text states**, then climb through about 8.1, 8.6 to about 9.0 at the next
252	Games, ending below the younger group's 10.0. This is a text-vs-figure inconsistency
253	of the same kind found in the Chapter 3 review (Fig. 3.10's "69.3%" versus the plotted
254	value); it is recorded here rather than silently resolved. The qualitative pattern the text
255	describes, older athletes drop, then climb back more slowly than they descended,
256	finishing below younger athletes, matches the figure regardless of the exact percentage.
257	
258	Table 4.5 (PDF p. 147, printed p. 136; verified against the page image) generalizes this
259	across the whole career, not just the first quadrennial year: **total training volume**
260	10-30% less than younger athletes ("older athletes train more conscientiously and
261	produce longer training residuals"); **annual cycle structure**: longer transition
262	period ("additional time for psychological and medical rehabilitation"); **organizational
263	forms**: higher share of individual (vs. group) training ("aged athletes need less
264	supervision, show more initiative and independence"); **restoration**: increased use of
265	restorative means ("older athletes recover slower and often suffer from previous
266	injuries"); **equipment**: more insistent, creative selection ("their own demands...
267	serious and consistent during their examination"); **individual progress**: "motor
268	potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively," i.e. "stabilization and
269	reduction of several functions are compensated for by higher efficiency of athletic
270	activity."
271	
272	**Why it works** — The author gives no physiological mechanism for the biological
273	"approaching their limits" claim beyond naming it; the entry that follows in Table 4.5
274	attributes the compensating higher performance to behavioral factors (conscientiousness,
275	individualized training, restoration, equipment care) and to "higher efficiency of
276	athletic activity" rather than to any stated biological process. **Inference:** this
277	pairs naturally with this library's existing residual-training-effect material: a more
278	trained system plausibly needs a smaller absolute training dose to hold a given
279	adaptation, but Issurin does not make that specific connection in this passage.
280	
281	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college roster** — A fifth-year or
282	graduate-transfer player entering a new coaching cycle, offseason, or scheme after
283	several years in a program is a rough structural analogue to Issurin's "experienced
284	athlete entering a new quadrennial cycle": expect (and program for) a lower initial
285	training volume than a true freshman or new transfer, a longer individualized
286	restoration/return-to-training window, and a training emphasis on utilization and
287	technical/tactical efficiency over raw volume increases, consistent with Table 4.5's
288	"motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."
289	
290	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** this is Issurin's own applied
291	generalization about elite, Olympic-cycle, mostly-individual-sport athletes typically in
292	their late 20s to 30s; it is not derived from a controlled or longitudinal study with
293	football-specific data, and "older" in this context (returning multi-Olympiad veterans)
294	does not map cleanly onto a 22-23-year-old college fifth-year player, whose biological
295	age is nowhere near the "biological limits" the text describes for career-long elite
296	athletes. The 15-20%/10-30% figures are the author's own stated bands, not derived
297	from a cited dataset in this passage, and (per the figure check above) the book's own
298	chart does not match its own 15-20% claim for the first-year drop.
299	
300	**Example** — **Inference:** a fifth-year offensive lineman returning after a coaching
301	staff or scheme change is deliberately started at a lower total training-volume target
302	than the incoming freshman class, with a longer individualized ramp and an emphasis
303	on technical efficiency (leverage, hand placement, pass-set footwork) rather than
304	chasing the volume numbers of his own earlier seasons, consistent with the
305	"motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively" framing.

325	# Klementiev: Training Volume Fell for 19 Years While Podium Results Kept Coming
326	
327	**What it is** — A single-athlete, 19-year longitudinal case: Ivan Klementiev, USSR
328	then Latvian Olympic canoeist, competed across four Olympic cycles, earning one gold
329	and two silver Olympic medals and seven World Championship golds (PDF p. 148,
330	printed p. 137). His total annual paddling volume was tracked by age (Figure 4.6, PDF
331	p. 149, printed p. 138; **verified against the page image**: the chart's peak at age 21,
332	roughly 4,900 km, matches the text's "maximal training volume was attained at age 21
333	when he trained with the USSR national squad"; volume then oscillates with periodic
334	late-quadrennial upticks but trends down through the following years, with the lowest
335	point at age 37, about 1,500 km). Issurin quantifies the decline by quadrennial-cycle
336	average, relative to the first cycle as 100%: **ages 21-24 = 100%; ages 25-28 = 88.2%;
337	ages 29-32 = 77.4%; ages 33-36 = 61%** (PDF p. 148, printed p. 137; text quote).
338	Transition periods lengthened over the same span, "from one to three months during
339	his career." Despite the steady volume decline, "after age 30 [he] won four gold medals
340	at the World Championships and two Olympic silver medals" (PDF p. 149, printed p.
341	138). Issurin's own conclusion: "workload reduction was effectively compensated for
342	by a higher quality of training," which he associates with the athlete's own account
343	(Klementiev, 1994) of "better preparation exploiting Block Periodization, a more
344	conscious and effective selection of exercises, avoidance of non-compatible workload
345	combinations, constant attention to restoration, and the use of a logical program of
346	competition." One deviation in the record is flagged as non-methodological: at age 24
347	(1984), "because of political, not methodological circumstances," Klementiev raced a
348	substitute regatta of socialist countries rather than the Los Angeles Olympics, cutting
349	that season short by a month (Figure 4.6 caption, PDF p. 149, printed p. 138).
350	
351	**Why it works** — The author's own causal claim ("workload reduction was
352	effectively compensated for by a higher quality of training") is stated, not
353	demonstrated: no comparison group, no measured "training quality" variable, and no
354	separation of the Block Periodization approach from the other listed factors (exercise
355	selection, compatibility management, restoration, competition-program logic) or from
356	simple accumulated technical/tactical experience. **The author gives no mechanism**
357	connecting reduced kilometers specifically to Block Periodization as opposed to any
358	other explanation for late-career success, including selection effects (an athlete who
359	stays competitive to age 36 across four Olympiads is, by construction, one of the rare
360	athletes for whom this pattern worked).
361	
362	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — Useful as a
363	citable, named-athlete illustration that declining training volume is not, by itself,
364	evidence of declining performance capacity in an experienced athlete, and that
365	tracking quality/specificity of training rather than raw volume may be the more
366	relevant monitoring question for a veteran player. Pairs directly with
367	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]]'s Table
368	4.5 claim that "motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."
369	
370	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is an n = 1, uncontrolled,
371	retrospective case with no comparison athlete who trained at a constant or rising
372	volume across the same span; it cannot separate the effect of reduced volume, Block
373	Periodization specifically, accumulated technical mastery, opponent turnover, or
374	survivorship (only athletes who remained competitive despite aging appear in this kind
375	of retrospective record; athletes for whom volume reduction did not work are absent
376	from it by definition). It is also a single elite paddler in an individual, cyclic-endurance
377	Olympic sport with a fixed quadrennial target; nothing here generalizes to a college
378	football roster's age range (18-23), position-specific demands, or annual (not
379	quadrennial) competitive cycle. Do not cite this case as evidence that reducing training
380	volume improves or preserves performance in general.
381	
382	**Example** — **Inference:** when a program has a small number of veteran players
383	whose measured training volumes are trending down year over year, Klementiev's case
384	is a reason to check training quality, technical execution, and competition-readiness
385	markers before treating the volume decline itself as a red flag, rather than a license to
386	assume volume reduction is automatically beneficial.
387

404	# Armstrong's Seven-Point Physiology Case: Read Only With the Doping Context the 2008 Book Does Not Give
405	
406	**Historical context absent from the source, stated first because it governs how the
407	rest of this entry should be read:** this book was published in 2008. Lance Armstrong
408	was stripped of all seven Tour de France titles (1999-2005) by the USADA "Reasoned
409	Decision" in 2012, following a finding of systematic doping (EPO, blood transfusions,
410	testosterone, corticosteroids) across the span this case study covers. That finding is not
411	in this book and could not have been reflected in it. This is stated as historical fact, not
412	as this entry-writer's opinion or as Eric's judgment; it is not labeled "Inference" because
413	it is not a reasoned inference from the text but an external, independently documented
414	fact about the case's subject. It means the physiological changes below cannot be read
415	as evidence of natural, doping-free long-term adaptation, and the case should not be
416	cited in that way.
417	
418	**What it is** — Issurin presents cyclist Lance Armstrong as a case study in long-term
419	physiological change, based on Coyle (2005), a published laboratory case-report of
420	serial testing from age 21 to 28 (PDF p. 150, printed p. 139; text quote): "From ages 21
421	to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body composition, maximal
422	oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical efficiency of pedaling." At age 24
423	he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and underwent surgery and a two-year course
424	of treatment including chemotherapy; from ages 27-32 he won the Tour de France six
425	times (per the book's count at time of writing). Over the seven-year span, body weight
426	rose slightly (+0.8 kg) while lean body weight rose more (+1.1 kg). **Verified against
427	the page image (Figure 4.7, PDF p. 151, printed p. 140):** the chart is two twin-axis
428	panels across nine unevenly spaced age points (21.1, 21.4, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28), a
429	hollow-star marker flagging the "medical treatment including chemotherapy" period
430	around age 24-25. Top panel: Heart Rate (left axis, 196-208 beats/min) and VO2max
431	(right axis, 60-85 ml/kg/min); bottom panel: mechanical efficiency (right axis,
432	20-23.5%) and power output at a VO2 of 5 L/min (left axis, 370-420 W), the latter two
433	rising together and roughly linearly across all nine points. The two top-panel series are
434	not unambiguously distinguishable from the rendered image alone (their in-panel labels
435	sit near line peaks without a clear leader-line to one series), so the values below are
436	taken from the book's stated text, not read independently off the chart: **maximum
437	heart rate decreased by 6 beats/min** over the seven years; **VO2max "reached peak
438	value at age 23, declined after medical treatment and did not reach the highest level
439	until age 28"**; **mechanical efficiency increased by 8.8%**; **power output at 5 L/min
440	VO2 increased by 18%**. The book flags that Armstrong's final VO2max, 71 ml/kg/min,
441	is "inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 ml/kg/min
442	(Padilla et al., 2000)," and speculates this partly reflects body-weight reduction before
443	races raising relative VO2max further than the absolute lab value shows. Issurin's stated
444	conclusion: "the individual progress of this great athlete was determined not by
445	enlargement of his physiological potential but by its more efficient utilization,"
446	listing hypothesized (not demonstrated) contributors: "pronounced hypertrophy and
447	improved contractility of slow muscle fibers, alteration in myosin ATPase activity,
448	increased cycling efficiency induced by altitude training and enhanced pedaling
449	technique" (PDF p. 150, printed p. 139). The book explicitly calls the "physiological
450	mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency... still unclear."
451	
452	**Why it works** — **The author gives no confirmed mechanism**; he states this
453	directly ("the physiological mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency is still
454	unclear") and lists candidate physiological explanations as speculative, not
455	established. **Inference (post-2012 context, not the book's):** the interpretation
456	problem is worse than an unresolved mechanism, because the underlying data-generating
457	process (systematic doping across this exact age-21-to-32 span, per USADA 2012) is
458	absent from both the book's account and from Coyle (2005), the primary source Issurin
459	cites. Any of the listed changes (mechanical efficiency, power at a fixed VO2, the
460	partial VO2max recovery after chemotherapy) could in principle be influenced by
461	doping practices not measured or disclosed in the primary source; this entry does not
462	assert that they were, only that the book's "individual creativity, self-confidence and
463	athletic wisdom" framing (PDF p. 151, printed p. 140) is not a complete account of the
464	known history.
465	
466	**When to apply** — Limited. The chemotherapy-recovery data point (VO2max
467	declining after cancer treatment, then partially recovering over several years) is the
468	one piece of this case with plausible standalone value, as an illustration that returning
469	to elite endurance performance after major medical treatment is a multi-year process,
470	not a single-season one. Do not use any other part of this case (the "better utilization,
471	not enlarged potential" conclusion, the specific percentage changes, the athlete as a
472	role model for long-term development) without disclosing the doping context above.
473	
474	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested**, and that ceiling is generous
475	given the context problem. This is an n = 1 case study, drawn from a primary source
476	(Coyle, 2005) that has itself drawn public scientific criticism for the same reason
477	(interpreting serial lab data from an athlete later found to have doped throughout the
478	tested period) independent of anything in this book. Do not cite Armstrong's
479	mechanical-efficiency or power gains as evidence for a "utilization, not enlargement"
480	training principle, and do not use this case in any coach- or athlete-facing material
481	without the 2012 finding attached. The Klementiev case
482	([[case-study--klementiev-multiyear-workload-decline-with-podium-longevity]]) is the
483	cleaner example of this book's "long-term progress through utilization, not raw
484	capacity" theme, without the same documented confound.
485	
486	**Example** — **Inference:** if this case is referenced at all in Applied Performance
487	material (e.g., illustrating return-to-elite-performance timelines after major medical
488	treatment), it should be paired with an explicit note on the athlete's subsequent USADA
489	finding, rather than presented as a clean physiology-of-aging or physiology-of-training
490	example.
491	
492	**Related** — [[case-study--klementiev-multiyear-workload-decline-with-podium-longevity]],
493	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].

508	# Four Stages of Long-Term Preparation, Dosed by Hours and Broken Out by Domain
509	
510	**What it is** — Issurin gives the same four-stage long-term development model
511	already in this library from Bompa
512	([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]), but adds two things
513	Bompa's entry does not have: an explicit dosing table and a domain-by-domain
514	(technical/physical/tactical/mental) content breakdown per stage. He opens by
515	scoping the topic down: "the athletic career... is highly dependent on the earlier period
516	of long-term preparation that usually begins in childhood. The purview of this chapter
517	restricts consideration of this matter, which is worthy of its own book" (PDF p. 152,
518	printed p. 141). Table 4.6 (PDF p. 152, printed p. 141; **verified against the page
519	image**: the raw text extraction of this table initially dropped a cell, recovered by
520	re-reading the rendered page) gives, per stage: **Preliminary preparation**: 1-3
521	years, 3-4 workouts/week, 45-60 min/workout, 120-170 hours/year; **Initial
522	specialization**: 2-3 years, 4-5 workouts/week, 75-90 min/workout, 250-300
523	hours/year; **Advanced specialization**: 2-3 years, 6-9 workouts/week, 60-120
524	min/workout, 500-750 hours/year; **Sports perfection**: duration "individually
525	dependent," 6-12 workouts/week, 70-150 min/workout, 750-1400 hours/year (cited to
526	Issurin, 1994). Favorable starting ages vary widely by sport (Figure 4.8, PDF p. 153,
527	printed p. 142; verified against the page image): gymnastics and figure skating
528	start roughly ages 7-9; swimming roughly 9-11; team/dual sports ("ball games"),
529	sprint track and field, weightlifting and fencing roughly 11-14; kayaking roughly
530	12-15; rowing roughly 13-16; marathon roughly 13-17; triathlon roughly 13-18
531	(adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, updated by expert interview). Issurin
532	notes the general trend toward earlier specialization across sport is driven by better
533	child-scaled equipment, training conditions, media popularization, and visible early
534	starters, and that these ranges reflect "worldwide practice" not individual exceptions
535	(PDF p. 153-154, printed p. 142-143).
536	
537	Each stage's content is broken out by four domains in Tables 4.7-4.10 (PDF pp.
538	154-157, printed pp. 143-146): **Preliminary preparation** (Table 4.7): technical:
539	sport-specific and general skill/coordination acquisition; physical: multilateral,
540	all-round development with sport-specific emphasis, raising general training capacity;
541	tactical: acquaintance with basic tactical demands; mental: consolidating interest,
542	forming motivation, "adoption of fundamental moral principles of 'fair play', team
543	spirit." **Initial specialization** (Table 4.8): technical: further sport-specific
544	development, selecting the most favorable discipline/event; physical: more specialized
545	motor-ability development, adapting to sport-typical workloads; tactical: deeper rules
546	and tactics knowledge; mental: self-confidence, will power, "consciousness and
547	responsibility." **Advanced specialization** (Table 4.9): technical: attaining effective,
548	individualized technique, eliminating technical drawbacks; physical: further
549	sport-specific motor-ability gains supporting individualized technique; tactical:
550	individualized tactical/techno-tactical formation; mental: motivation toward
551	excellence, emotional control, mental-regulation skill acquisition. Issurin adds a
552	caution here specific to this stage: "despite increased technical and motor abilities,
553	juniors at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads
554	should be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic
555	exercises requires complete control because highly qualified juniors can be overly
556	ambitious in their training routines but not experienced enough in self-regulation of
557	metabolic and muscular reactions" (PDF p. 155-156, printed p. 144-145). **Sports
558	perfection** (Table 4.10): technical: further enhancement with individual style;
559	physical: highest sport-specific ability level and its "improved utilization"; tactical:
560	tactical creativity, automatized favorite skills; mental: total commitment, highest
561	self-confidence, mood self-regulation, mental toughness. This fourth stage is "the most
562	variable in duration": "almost twenty years" for career-long stars like Klementiev and
563	Armstrong, "four-seven years" for most high-performance athletes (PDF p. 156, printed
564	p. 145).
565	
566	**A cross-source contradiction worth recording, not silently resolving:** this
567	library's Verkhoshansky/Supertraining entry
568	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]])
569	gives Soviet sport-school starting ages for some of the same sports that are
570	considerably earlier than Issurin's Figure 4.8 bands: women's gymnastics 4-5 vs.
571	Issurin's gymnastics 7-9; swimming 3-7 vs. Issurin's 9-11; weightlifting 10-11 vs.
572	Issurin's 11-14. Both tables are cited to different Soviet-era sources (Table 1.2 in
573	Supertraining is unsourced beyond "the Soviet sports-school system"; Figure 4.8 here
574	is adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, plus later expert interviews) and neither
575	book reconciles the gap. Record both; do not average them into a single number.
576	
577	**Why it works** — Issurin gives no outcome data for the dosing table (Table 4.6)
578	itself: no citation, no study comparing athletes trained at these hour/frequency bands
579	against alternative bands. **Inference:** the domain-by-domain content sequencing
580	(general before specific, tactical/mental development paced alongside physical)
581	matches this library's existing multilateral-before-specialization rationale
582	([[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]), but that
583	connection is this entry's own synthesis, not stated by Issurin in this passage.
584	
585	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a Baylor context** — The domain-by-domain
586	tables (4.7-4.10) are a usable template for structuring what "developmental content"
587	means at each career stage of a college program even though college football players
588	enter well past Issurin's "preliminary preparation" age band: an incoming freshman's
589	program content (movement-skill consolidation, general work capacity, tactical
590	acquaintance with the defense/offense) resembles the "initial specialization" /
591	"advanced specialization" domain mix more than "sports perfection," which better fits
592	an established starter. The advanced-specialization caution against maximal
593	anaerobic-glycolytic loading in not-yet-mature, "overly ambitious" young athletes is a
594	directly relevant caution for redshirt-freshman and true-freshman conditioning design.
595	
596	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** Table 4.6's specific
597	hour/frequency bands and Figure 4.8's starting ages are drawn from Olympic individual
598	and technical sports (gymnastics, swimming, rowing, weightlifting, etc.); American
599	football is not listed in either this table or the Verkhoshansky comparison table, and no
600	data source here addresses a contact team sport with a 100+ player roster and
601	heterogeneous training ages within a single class. The stage-duration bands are the
602	author's own applied synthesis (cited only to "Issurin, 1994," his own earlier work, not
603	an independent study), and the domain content lists, while plausible, carry no cited
604	outcome evidence distinguishing them from an alternative sequencing.
605	
606	**Example** — **Inference:** using Tables 4.7-4.8's domain content as a checklist for a
607	true-freshman's first developmental year: technical (movement-pattern competency
608	before position-specific technique refinement), physical (multilateral work capacity
609	before narrow specialization), tactical (scheme literacy before disguised assignments),
610	mental (culture and buy-in before performance-outcome pressure), while applying
611	Table 4.9's caution against maximal-intensity anaerobic-glycolytic work for players who
612	are still not fully mature and may be "overly ambitious" relative to their
613	self-regulation capacity.
614

633	
634	# Sensitive Periods: Ages Where a Motor Ability Trains Fastest, By Sex
635	
636	**What it is** — Issurin defines "sensitive periods" as ages when an individual is "more
637	trainable for certain motor abilities than in other times," resting on two stated
638	physiological facts (PDF p. 158, printed p. 147): (a) natural development of motor
639	abilities in children/youth is non-uniform, so sensitive periods yield "the most
640	favorable rate of improvement in certain abilities"; (b) acceleration/deceleration
641	periods for different abilities "do not coincide chronologically." He is explicit that
642	**chronological determination of sensitive periods "remains open to dispute"**: "each
643	fitness component can be characterized by various indices, which can give different
644	(and at times contradictory) chronological trends. This explains the variance in data
645	from different sources" (PDF p. 158, printed p. 147). Figure 4.9 (PDF p. 159, printed p.
646	148; **verified against the page image**, based on Meinel & Schnabel 1976, Martin
647	1980, Volkov 1986) plots the favorable-improvement window per ability, separately for
648	girls and boys, ages 8-18: general coordination roughly 9-12 for both sexes; flexibility
649	roughly 7-10 for both; speed (reaction time) roughly 9-11 for both; speed (movement
650	frequency) roughly 11-13 for both; explosive strength (high/long jump) roughly 11-13
651	in girls but extending to roughly 13-17 in boys; maximal strength roughly 13-17 in
652	girls, roughly 14-18 in boys; strength endurance roughly 11-14 in girls but extending to
653	roughly 11-17 in boys; aerobic endurance roughly 14-17 in girls, roughly 15-18 in
654	boys. The book's running text gives point estimates matching the chart: general
655	motor coordination peaks ages 9-12; flexibility ages 7-10; maximal-speed
656	improvement ages 11-13 in both sexes; reaction time ages 9-11; explosive-strength
657	(jump) improvement peaks 11-13 in girls, 13-17 in boys; aerobic-development
658	practice benefit ages 9-12, with the most favorable sensitive window from age 14 in
659	girls and 15 in boys.
660	
661	The chapter gives partial, explicitly qualified mechanisms for the strength-related
662	periods specifically (PDF pp. 159-160, printed pp. 148-149): jump performance
663	depends on "powerful muscular contractions and body mass," and body mass "increases
664	most noticeably in mid-puberty girls aged 13-15" while their maximal improvement
665	rate occurs earlier, at 11-13; strength gains in mid/late puberty are "directly affected
666	by hormonal changes (maturation) and an increase in muscle mass (growth)"; but
667	"training-induced hypertrophy is much more pronounced in adults in comparison to
668	mid-pubertal or late-pubertal children. Therefore, improvement in neural regulation is
669	the main source of increased explosive and maximal strength" in youth. Androgenic
670	hormones (e.g. testosterone), which "affect anaerobic power production and muscle
671	hypertrophy," are "low in children and only start to increase at ages 12-13 in girls, and
672	13-14 in boys." Aerobic-endurance sensitivity is attributed to "increased body size, and
673	in particular, muscle mass, increased heart volume, total blood volume, and a higher
674	hemoglobin concentration." The chapter closes this section with an explicit safety
675	caution: "the higher sensitivity of children and youth can lead to overload and even
676	injury. This is particularly relevant in training for maximum strength and in power
677	exercises" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149).
678	
679	**Why it works** — The neural-regulation-over-hypertrophy explanation for youth
680	strength gains, and the testosterone-onset ages for anaerobic power/hypertrophy, are
681	standard, independently established developmental physiology, consistent with this
682	library's existing maturation material; that specific mechanism claim can be treated at
683	the `proven` ceiling **for the underlying physiology itself** (androgen-driven
684	hypertrophic capacity rising at puberty; neural adaptation predominating over
685	hypertrophic adaptation before it). The overall age windows in Figure 4.9, however, stay
686	at `supported`: the author himself states the chronological boundaries are disputed
687	across sources, and the figure is a synthesis of three secondary citations (Meinel &
688	Schnabel 1976; Martin 1980; Volkov 1986), none independently checked in this ingest.
689	
690	**When to apply — Inference** — Directly relevant to Applied Performance's role in
691	any camp or clinic work with pre-collegiate athletes, and as background for
692	understanding why a college freshman's training-age deficits in particular abilities
693	(e.g., poor general coordination, limited flexibility) may reflect a missed
694	developmental window rather than a simply "untrained" quality that responds at the
695	same rate an early-developed quality would. The sex-specific timing differences
696	(explosive strength and strength endurance windows running longer in boys; aerobic
697	endurance starting a year later in boys than girls) are a concrete reference for
698	age-and-sex-differentiated youth programming, where Applied Performance interacts
699	with prospective-athlete or camp populations.
700	
701	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** every current Baylor
702	football player is already past every window shown in Figure 4.9 (which stops at age
703	18); this framework describes developmental timing, not a claim about how to train
704	already-matured collegiate athletes, and should not be used to argue that any current
705	ability gap is now unfixable. The author's own caveat applies directly: chronological
706	sensitive-period boundaries are disputed, vary by which index is measured, and come
707	from three secondary sources not independently verified here. Treat the specific age
708	ranges as a useful planning heuristic for youth-facing work, not a precise biological
709	clock.
710	
711	**Example** — **Inference:** a youth combine or camp screening tool that flags,
712	rather than penalizes, a 9-year-old with below-average flexibility or a 14-year-old boy
713	with below-average explosive-strength improvement rate as "inside a sensitive
714	window where targeted work is likely to pay off fastest," consistent with the chapter's
715	framing that these are periods of highest trainability, not fixed ceilings.
716	
717	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
718	[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
719	[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].
720	=================== framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model.md
721	---
722	type: library-entry
723	kind: framework
724	domain: strength-and-conditioning
725	book: block-periodization--issurin

729	confidence: supported

731	created: 2026-09-27
732	---
733	
734	# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are
735	
736	**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
737	trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
738	individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
739	printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
740	organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
741	(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
742	**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
743	(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
744	(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
745	orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
746	flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
747	concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
748	partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
749	background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
750	though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
751	necessary"). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
752	anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
753	such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
754	progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149): the high-heritability rows
755	function as hard constraints on which sports/positions an athlete can realistically excel
756	in, while the low-heritability rows are the ones training and environment can move.
757	
758	The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
759	characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986): favorable anthropometric/physiological
760	combinations by age category, built from longitudinal study of a large athlete group
761	where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov et al. 1999 and Falk et al.
762	2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty), or more commonly from
763	cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful youngsters. Issurin flags
764	the model characteristics' central limitation directly: "the main limitation of this
765	evaluation is in the differing levels of maturity of children that are examined to
766	determine giftedness. Children with slower rates of maturation may be found inferior
767	to more mature teammates but may have greater potential for further progress" (PDF
768	p. 160, printed p. 149). Genetic contribution to training response itself is not constant
769	across a career: citing a young-adult twin study (Bouchard et al., 2000), "the
770	contribution of heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program
771	is different for earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less
772	dependent on heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads,
773	the genetic control of their training response becomes much stronger" (PDF p. 167,
774	printed p. 156), meaning genetically gifted endurance athletes can be genuinely hard
775	to identify at the earliest stage, not just hard to identify due to maturation confounds.
776	
777	**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
778	citation for most individual cells (the table itself has no source line beyond the
779	chapter's general references to Williams & Franks/Reilly); it functions as the author's
780	synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The twin
781	study citation (Bouchard et al., 2000) is the one mechanism-level claim in this section
782	with a named, checkable primary source, though it was not independently verified in
783	this ingest.
784	
785	**When to apply — Inference** — Directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
786	recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
787	Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
788	recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
789	from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
790	psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
791	direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
792	"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
793	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].
794	
795	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** this taxonomy and its
796	heritability gradings are drawn from Olympic individual-sport talent-ID research
797	(swimming, track, rowing-type literature per the cited authors); American football's
798	position-specific demands are not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-
799	specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
800	qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
801	author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
802	maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
803	and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
804	mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.
805	
806	**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
807	when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
808	profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
809	flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
810	sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
811	relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
812	here as real, modifiable contributors to development.
813	
814	**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]],
815	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
816	[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
817	[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].
818	=================== heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness.md
819	---
820	type: library-entry
821	kind: heuristic
822	domain: strength-and-conditioning
823	book: block-periodization--issurin
824	chapter: "4.4.3"
825	topic: identifying giftedness via initial level and improvement rate
826	category: [youth, talent-identification, testing]
827	confidence: supported
