# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite

**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
analysis. **Verified against the page image (Figure 4.10, PDF p. 163, printed p. 152):**
performance time on a 500-m course is plotted by two-year age band (14-15 through
18-19) for three groups (kayak-males, kayak-females, canoeists), all three showing a
steep improvement curve from roughly 140-152 seconds at 14-15 down to roughly
102-120 seconds by 18-19, with kayak-males consistently fastest across every age band
and kayak-females and canoeists tracking close together. The book frames the result as
a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
p. 163, printed p. 152).

**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model (no reported correlation,
sensitivity, or false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen
today's youngsters). Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.

**When to apply — Inference** — As a template, not as transferable numbers: the
approach of interviewing an already-elite cohort about their own performance at a
fixed early-career age point, to build a retrospective reference curve for evaluating
today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
specific canoe-kayak times. It illustrates the general "model characteristics" approach
named earlier in the chapter (Bulgakova, 1986,
[[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]) with a concrete worked
example of how such a benchmark curve is actually built and reported.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
the time of interview, so the study cannot say what fraction of 14-15-year-olds with
similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no comparison group of
similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also sport- and era-specific
(1970s-80s Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, pre-modern boat and
paddle equipment) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** the method (not the numbers) could be adapted for a
sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their
own testing numbers at a fixed early developmental checkpoint (e.g. end of a true
freshman year), building an internal reference curve for how "what elite eventually
looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect, while explicitly
tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
many similarly-scoring peers did not.

**Related** — [[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

lines: +type: library-entry
+kind: framework
+domain: strength-and-conditioning
+book: science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky
+chapter: "2"
+topic: resistance types and equipment selection
+category: [equipment-selection, biomechanics, exercise-selection]
+confidence: supported
+ingest-tier: full-text
+# Five Types of Mechanical Resistance, and Why Equipment Choice Can Break Sport-Movement Specificity
+**What it is** — Resistance training equipment can be classified by the physical law
+governing the resistance it provides: **elasticity** (F = k₁D; force proportional to
+displacement/deformation D, coefficient k₁ = stiffness — springs, stretch cords, rubber
+bands; force is greatest at the end of range, when deformation is largest); **inertia**
+(Newton's second law, F = ma; force proportional to the mass being accelerated — hard to
+isolate purely inertial resistance outside lab devices like an inertia wheel, since gravity
+and friction intrude); **weight** (F = W + ma, W = object weight, a = vertical
+acceleration); **hydrodynamic resistance** (F = k₂V², proportional to velocity squared —
+swimming, rowing, kayaking); and **viscosity-based resistance** (F = k₃V, proportional to
+velocity, k₃ = a coefficient — used in machines substituting for water-sport dryland
+training). Exercises are also classified by whether they have **mechanical feedback**: in a
+paddling stroke, higher muscular force raises oar velocity, which raises water resistance,
+which in turn demands more muscular force (a closed loop, figure 2.4) — most sport
+movements have this feedback loop. Mechanical feedback is **absent** specifically in
+isometric exercise and with isokinetic devices (constant velocity regardless of force
+applied), which is why those modes do not reproduce most sport movements' natural
+force-resistance interaction. (PDF pp. 30-31, 33-34, 51-52, printed pp. 21, 23-24, 42-43.)
+**Why it works** — Inference: because different sport movements are naturally resisted by
+different physical laws (hydrodynamic for swimming, elastic/momentum-based for most
+throwing and jumping, weight-and-inertia for lifting), an exercise's resistance type
+determines how closely its force-velocity demand matches the target movement, independent
+of which muscles it uses — this is the authors' own point in the dryland-training case
+study below, though the general "resistance type governs specificity" framing is this
+entry's synthesis of the mechanics they lay out.
+**When to apply** — As a checklist when selecting resistance training equipment intended to
+transfer to a specific sport skill: match the resistance-type profile (elastic, inertial,
+weight-based, hydrodynamic, viscosity-based) to the target movement's actual resistance
+type, not just its visible muscle groups or general movement pattern. This complements
+[[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]] (Chapter 1) by giving a
+mechanical reason, in addition to a measured-transfer-coefficient reason, that an exercise
+might fail to transfer.
+**When NOT to apply** — Inference: this is a mechanics-based classification, not itself a
+ranked hierarchy of "better" and "worse" resistance types; each type is appropriate for
+different training goals (elastic resistance for end-range loading, isokinetic/isometric
+for eliminating the confound of a changing external load during rehab-style force testing,
+despite lacking mechanical feedback). Do not treat "lacks mechanical feedback" as
+disqualifying isometric or isokinetic training outright; the authors present it as a
+descriptive difference from most sport movements, not a stated flaw.
+**Example** — The authors' own case study, "Selection of Dryland Exercises for Swimmers"
+(printed p. 25): a swim coach trialed extensible rubber bands (elastic resistance, pulling
+force increased through the pull, unlike the customary stroke), a weightlifting pulley
+machine (near-constant resistance across the pull, but the athletes could not relax at the
+end of motion, unlike a real stroke), and friction/hydrodynamic training devices (either
+constant resistance or resistance proportional to pull velocity, both meant to mimic water
+resistance) — none matched the true stroke's resistance profile (proportional to the
+squared hand velocity relative to water) exactly, illustrating why matching a device's
+underlying resistance law to the sport movement's own is harder than it looks, even when
+targeting the same muscle groups and general movement pattern.
+**Related** — [[framework--transfer-of-training-coefficient-calculation]],
+[[claim--strength-speed-correlation-depends-on-external-resistance]].

495	compulsory component of the annual program in early-, mid- and late season and a 
496	varied program of competition helps to diversify the training routine and restore

499	4.2 Quadrennial cycle of athletic preparation 
500	 
501	 
502	Completion of the Olympic quadrennial cycle is usually followed by serious 
503	and detailed analysis of the Olympic performance including successes and failures. It 
504	is natural for great success to elicit enthusiasm and inspiration and for failure to cause 
505	dissatisfaction, criticism and a tendency to reform. Irrespective of sport-specificity 
506	and nationality, the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to internalize positive 
507	experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based on the findings, a 
508	new preparatory plan is worked out. It is good when clear and concrete general 
509	objectives are determined for each stage of the quadrennial plan. An example of 
510	setting objectives can be found in the preparation of one of the most successful 
511	gymnastics team of Russia (Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004).

523	Example. The quadrennial cycle of the Russian gymnastics national team is 
524	subdivided into eight half-year stages.  Each stage is directed to a specific general 
525	objective:  
526	1. 
527	Enhancement of sport-specific motor fitness 
528	2. 
529	Acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and their hybrids 
530	3. 
531	Updating of combinations used in competition 
532	4. 
533	Further increases in sport-specific motor fitness 
534	5. 
535	Enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable (reliable) performances 
536	6. 
537	Increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance. 
538	7. 
539	Final compilation of competition combinations, development of endurance for 
540	an entire program and selection of a duplicate Olympic squad 
541	8. 
542	Modeling of expected competitive conditions, attaining high competitive 
543	reliability and final selection of the Olympic National team.

841	Case study of physiological changes during long-term preparation. Lance 
842	Armstrong, world famous cyclist, became World Champion and seven-time Grand 
843	Champion of the Tour de France, the most famous and prestigious road race in the 
844	world. From ages 21 to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body 
845	composition, maximal oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical 
846	efficiency of pedaling. At age 24 he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and 
847	during a two year period he came through surgery and treatment that included 
848	chemotherapy. From ages 27-32 Lance Armstrong was victorious six times in the 
849	Tour de France, undoubtedly an incredible success in world sport. 
850	           During a seven year period, starting from age 21, the athlete's body weight 
851	increased slightly by 0.8 kg while lean body weight increased by 1.1 kg. The 
852	multi-year trend of physiological variables showed the following (Figure 4.7): 
853	- 
854	the maximum oxygen uptake reached peak value at age 23, declined after 
855	medical treatment and did not reach the highest level until age 28 when he won 
856	the Tour de France; 
857	- 
858	maximum heart rate decreased by 6 beat/min; 
859	- 
860	mechanical efficiency, as the ratio of mechanical work to energy expended, 
861	increased by 8.8%; 
862	- 
863	mechanical power obtained at an oxygen uptake of 5.0 l/min displayed a 
864	substantial increase of 18%. 
865	It is worth noting that the final estimate of maximum oxygen uptake, 71 
866	ml/kg/min, is inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 
867	ml/kg/min (Padilla et al., 2000). It can be speculated that when Lance reduced his 
868	body weight prior to the races, the real level of maximum oxygen uptake per body 
869	weight became higher than previously. Nevertheless the study findings indicate 
870	that the individual progress of this great athlete was determined not by 
871	enlargement of his physiological potential but by its more efficient utilization. The 
872	physiological mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency is still unclear. 
873	The hypothetical contributors to such improvement can be associated with 
874	pronounced hypertrophy and improved contractility of slow muscle fibers, 
875	alteration in myosin ATPase activity, increased cycling efficiency induced by 
876	altitude training and enhanced pedaling technique.

1273	4.4.2 Sensitive periods in the development of different motor abilities  
1274	  
1275	Both researchers and practitioners have remarked that during certain periods in 
1276	an individuals life they are more trainable for certain motor abilities than in other 
1277	times. These time periods have been termed “sensitive periods” and are based on the 
1278	following physiological facts:  
1279	 
1280	a) The natural development of physical (motor) abilities and physiological 
1281	functions in children and youth is non-uniform.  The sensitive periods 
1282	make it possible to make more progress and have the most favorable rate 
1283	of improvement in certain abilities;  
1284	b)  The periods of acceleration and deceleration of motor development for 
1285	different abilities do not coincide chronologically.  Some of them occur 
1286	earlier, others – later. 
1287	  
1288	 
1289	Non-uniformity and chronological heterogeneity in the development of 
1290	various motor abilities are widely known phenomena. However, chronological 
1291	determination of the sensitive periods with regard to specific motor abilities remains 
1292	open to dispute.  Each fitness component can be characterized by various indices, 
1293	which can give different (and at times contradictory) chronological trends. This 
1294	explains the variance in data from different sources. Other approaches entail 
1295	comparing training-induced effects achieved at different ages. Using this approach, 
1296	the sensitive periods were determined and are shown in Figure 4.9. 
1297	 
1298	In general, the sensitive periods are determined by growth, maturation and 
1299	natural trends in the development of the motor system. Physical activity and specially 
1300	organized training are integrative factors that stimulate and augment the natural 
1301	physical trend. For instance, the most favorable period for improvement of general 
1302	motor coordination is between ages 9-12.  Coordinated ability increases at an older 
1303	age as well, but its improvement rate is lower. Similarly, flexibility increases 
1304	considerably more at ages 7-10 when the high elasticity of tendons, ligaments and 
1305	joints is beneficial for making progress. The elementary forms of speed also develop 
1306	non-uniformly.  The highest improvement rate for maximal movement speed occurs 
1307	at ages 11-13 in both girls and boys while reaction time improves most at 9-11 years 
1308	of age.

1340	The influence of growth and maturation is especially pronounced with regard 
1341	to strength abilities. Achievements in the high- and long jump depends on powerful 
1342	muscular contractions and body mass. The latter component increases most noticeably 
1343	in mid-puberty girls aged 13-15; and their maximal improvement rate occurs at 11-13. 
1344	 
1345	Boys perform better in the high- and long jumps at ages 13-17. The 
1346	improvement in maximal strength attained in mid-puberty and late-puberty is directly 
1347	affected by hormonal changes (maturation) and an increase in muscle mass (growth). 
1348	It is well known that improvement in muscle strength is a result of better neural 
1349	regulation as well as muscular hypertrophy. It is worth noting that training-induced 
1350	hypertrophy is much more pronounced in adults in comparison to mid-pubertal or 
1351	late-pubertal children. Therefore, improvement in neural regulation is the main source 
1352	of increased explosive and maximal strength. Improvement in neural adaptation also 
1353	contributes to gains in strength endurance. Other contributors relate to metabolic 
1354	factors (aerobic and anaerobic energy supply) and hormonal aspects. More 
1355	specifically, the androgenic hormones (e.g., testosterone) affect anaerobic power

1378	4.4.3 Identifying gifted athletes 
1379	 
1380	 
1381	In general, giftedness can be characterized as a predisposition to and a higher 
1382	trainability for a given activity.  These are considered to be genetically transmitted 
1383	properties of an individual. In sports, properly developing giftedness implies attaining 
1384	sports excellence. Apparently, the earlier this giftedness is identified, the more 
1385	effectively the individual's athletic preparation can be managed and the greater is the 
1386	probability of developing an elite athlete. Thus, a gifted child is potentially a talented 
1387	athlete and, therefore, identification of giftedness can be based on unchangeable 
1388	inherited predictors of talent.  
1389	 
1390	According to the current approach (Williams & Franks, 1998; Williams & 
1391	Reilly, 2000), sport talent is determined by four generalized factors: anthropometrical, 
1392	physiological, psychological and sociological.  Each of them contains numerous 
1393	characteristics that can serve as predictors of potential talent. Some anthropometrical 
1394	and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as such, can not be 
1395	compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict progress in a given 
1396	sport. Several psychological personality traits are somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 
1397	1994; Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation. Sociological

1458	The identification of gifted, that is, potentially talented athletes, can be based 
1459	on unchangeable predictors, most often associated with anthropometric and

1461	characteristics, which describe favorable combinations of anthropometric and 
1462	physiological measurements for different age categories (Bulgakova, 1986). The 
1463	characteristics were used for identifying candidates with the best prospects for 
1464	benefiting from more specialized training. The main limitation of this evaluation is in 
1465	the differing levels of maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. 
1466	Children with slower rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature 
1467	teammates but may have greater potential for further progress.

1476	Special attention should be given to determining the most favorable 
1477	combinations of anthropometric and physiological estimates for different ages. Such 
1478	age related models can be created through longitudinal study of a large group of 
1479	athletes, where one sub-group attains the elite level. Data for the athletes recorded in 
1480	the different periods can be used as model characteristics for corresponding age 
1481	categories. It is obvious that such a study, which would take a number of years, 
1482	appears difficult and has organizational problems, but such long-term research 
1483	projects have been conducted (Vorontsov et al. 1999; Falk et al., 2003). Much more 
1484	common are so-called cross-sectional studies that compare less successful and more 
1485	successful youngsters.  The results are used to reveal some specifics about 
1486	hypothetically gifted athletes.

1702	Summary 
1703	 
1704	Long-term athletic preparation has been considered with respect to designing 
1705	relatively prolonged training cycles (annual and quadrennial), multi-year preparation 
1706	of adult, and multi-year preparation of young athletes. The basics of annual cycle 
1707	construction included goals and objectives, sequencing the main steps in the annual 
1708	plan, and general tendencies in workload compilation. All these items are considered 
1709	in light of the Block Periodization concept.  
1710	 
1711	Special attention was given to seasonal trends in training workloads within the 
1712	annual cycle of preparation (Table 4.3). Particulars regarding quadrennial planning 
1713	were given for preparing highly qualified athletes. Special attention was given to 
1714	workload trends in preparing older and experienced athletes and their younger 
1715	counterparts. Also, the problem of athletic longevity was briefly analyzed with respect 
1716	to the characteristics of the older experienced athletes (Table 4.5).  
1717	
1718

1720	157
1721	 
1722	 
1723	 
1724	The typical trend in annual training workloads was presented together with a 
1725	case study of many-time world and Olympic canoeing champion Ivan Klementiev 
1726	(Latvia), while physiological changes during long-term preparation were considered 
1727	on the basis of a case study of World Champion and seven-time Tour de France 
1728	champion, Lance Armstrong (USA). It was seen that many older athletes approach 
1729	their biological limits but continue to attain outstanding performances, and even 
1730	improve their athletic results. The source of such individual progress can be attributed 
1731	to better utilization of their motor and physiological capabilities, where individual 
1732	creativity, self-confidence and athletic wisdom play a big role.  
1733	 
1734	 
1735	The common approach to long-term athletic preparation assumes there are 
1736	four separate stages.  They are preliminary preparation, initial specialization,  
1737	advanced specialization, and sports perfection. Each of these is characterized by the 
1738	proper combination of stage length, frequency and duration of workouts, yearly 
1739	training volume and other sport-specific variables. The physical, technical, tactical 
1740	and mental characteristics of each stage were summarized and considered in general 
1741	(Tables 4.7-4.10). 
1742	 
1743	In terms of biological maturation, the concept of sensitive periods is of special 
1744	importance. It assumes there are the periods in an individuals life when they are more 
1745	trainable for certain motor abilities than at other times. Consequently, the periods of 
1746	most favorable training responses can be exploited for more conscientious and 
1747	beneficial development (Figure 4.9). Special attention was given to the identification 
1748	of gifted young athletes, because early identification of giftedness permits more 
1749	effective management of preparation in talented athletes with great potential. 
1750	Prospective and retrospective approaches for determining valid and informative 
1751	indicators of giftedness were considered. For practical purposes and general 
1752	evaluation of giftedness, it is highly recommended that the initial level of sport-
1753	specific fitness characteristics be evaluated as a predisposition to a given sport.  The 
1754	improvement rate of athletic abilities during initial preparation should be evaluated as 
1755	an indicator of trainability. The comprehensive scheme presented in Figure 4.12 
1756	makes it possible to estimate athletic giftedness in general.

1850	Altitude training has been a greatly disputed topic in sports science and of 
1851	much interest to researchers and coaches for over three decades. Generally speaking, 
1852	the present situation is paradoxical. Publications written for coaches consider altitude 
1853	training to be an efficacious and proven tool for enhancing high-level performance 
1854	(Fuchs & Reiss, 1990; Dick, 1992; Suslov et al., 1999) while exercise physiology 
1855	textbooks and professional reviews state that altitude training provides no extra 
1856	benefits for sea level performance than conventional training (Jensen & Fisher,1979;  
1857	McArdle et al., 1991; Wilmore & Costill, 1993; Saltin, 1996, inter alia).  
1858	 
1859	From a practical viewpoint, the positive experiences of prominent coaches, 
1860	great athletes and several national teams, offer strong arguments for employing 
1861	altitude training.  Many successful national teams, particularly in the endurance 
1862	sports, incorporate altitude training as part of their preparation. This chapter 
1863	summarizes the current body of physiological and methodological data concerning 
1864	altitude training with respect to training program design. The scientific background 
1865	presented here is limited and readers are advised to refer to other sources (see reviews 
1866	of Boning et al., 1997; Rusko et al., 2004; Wilber, 2004 and others).

Long-term preparation concerns periods lasting one year and more. From this 
viewpoint three major aspects of long-term preparation demand proper consideration.  
They are the annual cycle, multi-year preparation of qualified athletes, including the 
quadrennial cycle, and multi-year preparation of juniors. This chapter will present and 
clarify the basic positions and planning guidelines pertaining to these three aspects.  
 
4.1 The annual cycle 
 
The planning of the annual cycle in terms of Block Periodization was 
previously described in general terms. Special attention should be given to the 
technology of planning and guidelines for training design.   
 
4.1.1 Goals, objectives and basic directions of the annual plan  
 
 
When dealing with experienced athletes, annual goal setting and establishing 
objectives frequently seem superfluous. Even a brief analysis, however, will show that 
they are important. Goal setting for annual preparation demonstrates the coach's 
responsibility and stimulates athletes to undertake serious obligations. Concrete

training objectives indicate the gains in technique, motor fitness, mental toughness 
etc. that should be made in order to attain the main goal. The motivation and 
confidence of the athletes will be higher and more stable when they can clearly see 
the ways in which the annual preparation can be made more effective (use of new 
training methods, enhanced monitoring, employment of new equipment etc.). And 
finally, the coach and athlete should discover the athlete’s hidden reserves, which 
when liberated, will facilitate better performance (Table 4.1).

Unfortunately not every season ends successfully.  In such cases the coach 
starts planning for the next year by analyzing the failures that occurred. The simplest 
way of conducting such an analysis is by seeking the external fatal factors affecting 
the athletes’ performance. The array of possible fatal reasons is large: bad draw, low 
judgment, sudden wind or rain, earthquake etc. A tactic employed by a great coach, is 
to explain to unsuccessful athletes that the training program was excellent and that 
they (the athletes) were completely responsible for the failure.  The correct approach 
to analysis assumes mutual responsibility of coach and athlete for both successful and 
unsuccessful seasons. This is important in order for the athletes to develop a confident 
attitude in regard to goal setting for the next season.

The next step in annual planning is the calculation of integrative monthly 
workload characteristics. Parameters such as total number of workouts, total mileage, 
number of bouts and matches, number of quasi-competitive performances etc. can be 
successfully planned per month. The summation of all the monthly characteristics 
yields the integrative annual workloads, which can then be compared with previous 
years and the data of other athletes. Usually this whole planning process does not lead 
to the final version of annual program. It must first be reviewed by the administration, 
colleagues and athletes and with repeated analysis, will lead to corrections in specific 
details such as the timing and duration of training camps, cancellation of competitions 
etc. The corrected program then receives the final version status that is used for 
realization. 
 
4.1.3 General trends in workload planning within the annual cycle of 
preparation 
 
 
The general tendency in annual planning is to reserve the most specialized and 
rigorous workloads for the training period preceding the most important competition. 
The Block Periodization approach with its multi-peak preparation does not contradict 
this position although it exploits it in its own way. 


######## IDX 142
131

several common trends in program compilation can be seen (Table 4.3).

The general tendency is to gradually increase workload specialization and 
mobilization of hidden reserves towards the target competition. The general rule in 
Block Periodization is that the training stages within the annual cycle should be 
similar but not identical. The mid season and particularly late season stages should be 
more rigorous, more strictly programmed and better managed. It is highly desirable 
that the most effective training and restorative means and drill combinations be 
reserved for the crucial periods in annual preparation. Physiologically, this gives the 
benefit of higher training responses prior to the most important events.  
Psychologically, it heightens the athletes' self-confidence as they know that they have 
additional reserves during the most stressful phase of their preparation.  
 
 


######## IDX 143
132
 
 
Special attention should be given to the competitive component of annual 
preparation. Block Periodization gives great importance to competitions even in the 
early phase of the annual cycle for the following reasons:  
1) competition completes each training stage and is a compulsory component of 
the training program; 
2)  the competition breaks the usual routine and brings out the very important 
element of athlete spirit;  
3) the competition provides athletes with extraordinary training stimuli that can 
not be obtained from regular workloads. 
 
 It is worth noting that the competitive program varies during the season. It is 
good to diversify the competitions in early season, to bring the competition to event-
specific standards in mid season, and to adhere to event-specific standards in late 
season. The reasons for such changes are two-fold.  The competitions are a 
compulsory component of the annual program in early-, mid- and late season and a 
varied program of competition helps to diversify the training routine and restore 
athletes after the habitual event-specific format.   
 
4.2 Quadrennial cycle of athletic preparation 
 
 
Completion of the Olympic quadrennial cycle is usually followed by serious 
and detailed analysis of the Olympic performance including successes and failures. It 
is natural for great success to elicit enthusiasm and inspiration and for failure to cause 
dissatisfaction, criticism and a tendency to reform. Irrespective of sport-specificity 
and nationality, the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to internalize positive 
experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based on the findings, a 
new preparatory plan is worked out. It is good when clear and concrete general 
objectives are determined for each stage of the quadrennial plan. An example of 
setting objectives can be found in the preparation of one of the most successful 
gymnastics team of Russia (Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004). 
 
 
 
 
 


######## IDX 144
133
 
 
Example. The quadrennial cycle of the Russian gymnastics national team is 
subdivided into eight half-year stages.  Each stage is directed to a specific general 
objective:  
1. 
Enhancement of sport-specific motor fitness 
2. 
Acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and their hybrids 
3. 
Updating of combinations used in competition 
4. 
Further increases in sport-specific motor fitness 
5. 
Enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable (reliable) performances 
6. 
Increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance. 
7. 
Final compilation of competition combinations, development of endurance for 
an entire program and selection of a duplicate Olympic squad 
8. 
Modeling of expected competitive conditions, attaining high competitive 
reliability and final selection of the Olympic National team. 
Each of the above stages encompasses a complex evaluation of the cumulative 
training effect induced by the completed program. 
 
 
This example shows that dividing the quadrennial cycle into separate stages is 
a matter of professional competence and depends on sport-specific conditions. 
Nevertheless, the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual cycles is the most 
popular. In general, the main directions of quadrennial preparation, irrespective of 
sport, are presented in Table 4.4.   
 
Table 4.4

1st

other staff specialists, updating and correcting usual training means and 
methods, remodeling training repertory, formation of team spirit and 
camaraderie between athletes and staff. 
2nd

tactical skills, increase in training workloads, improving quality of training 
3rd

planned for the Olympic season and determining the individual performance

stabilization of workloads on the level of the preceding year, approval and

######## IDX 145
134
 
 
 
Let's consider the above directions with respect to training designed for 
athletes of different ages and levels of experience. Highly experienced top-level 
athletes require special attention during Olympic preparation both on national teams 
of leading sports countries, where coaches enjoy a large number of potential athletes, 
and on relatively small national teams, where the possibility of adding new successful 
team-members is very limited. The advantages of older and experienced athletes are 
obvious as they have a remarkable advantage in terms of basic and sport-specific 
knowledge, emotional control, stability of technical, techno-tactical skills and 
competitive behavior. They are usually high-authority persons who positively affect 
social climate and team spirit.  
 
The disadvantages of having such athletes are also clear as they are 
approaching their biological limits in regard to training responses, i.e., they have less 
reactivity to training stimuli, they usually follow habitual training programs and do 
not like to change their training style and repertory. Older athletes perform with a 
lower training volume and need longer transition periods for physical and mental 
rehabilitation. In the first annual cycle of the quadrennial plan these athletes have a 
substantially lower total volume of exercises – about 15-20% less – than in the 
previous Olympic year (Figure 4.5).

Experienced, more aged athletes continue the quadrennial cycle with a gradual 
increase in training volume, which in any case is usually less than that for their 
younger counterparts. The model for the third annual cycle is based on the Olympic 
year for each category of athletes.  Both aged and younger athletes increase the level 
of their training workloads and approach their maximum. Generally speaking, the 
third and fourth annual cycles should be very similar since coaches simulate the 
annual pre-Olympic training design one year before in order to provide the highest 
quality preparation at the end stage of the quadrennial cycle. In fact, the training 
workload level in the pre-Olympic season is usually higher than the year before for 
various reasons.  This includes greater motivation, better conditions for training and 
restoration, greater budgets etc.  
 
 
Younger athletes, who have not participated in the Olympic Games have 
typical characteristics. After being involved in Olympic preparations, their athletic 
motivation is greatly stimulated and they usually enjoy better training conditions that 
include more training camps, more qualified training partners, sometimes more 
experienced coaches etc. As a result, these athletes substantially increase their training 
workloads in comparison to the previous year. In the second and third annual cycles 
the training workloads continue to rise although at a smaller rate of increase.  
 
 
From a methodological point of view, it is important to predict and plan 
development of the most relevant motor, technical and tactical abilities. For this, it is 
necessary to expand the corresponding model characteristics of these components of 
preparedness with respect to improvement rates during the quadrennial cycle.  
 
4.3  Sport longevity of highly qualified athletes 
 
 
Contemporary sport has many examples of highly successful athletes who 
continue their careers up to and past age thirty. This athletic longevity has been 
affected by many factors, such as high and stable motivation, proper style of behavior, 
improved training methodology, social support, financial stimulation, etc. In regard to 
the training itself, a number of age-related characteristics can be pinpointed 
irrespective of the sport involved (Table 4.5).

Of course, a number of additional social factors affect the preparation and 
behavior of aged athletes. Very often they combine their athletic preparation with 
professional activity and some odler athletes have families which substantially 
changes their mentality and life priorities. The preparation particulars can be 
illustrated using examples of two outstanding athletes who attained great results 
during their long athletic careers. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


######## IDX 148
137
 
 
Case study of long-term training workloads. The world-famous canoeist, 
Olympic Champion Ivan Klementiev represented the USSR and from 1991, 
Latvia during four Olympic cycles. He earned one gold and two silver 
Olympic medals and seven World Championship gold medals. During a 
period of 19 years many aspects of his training were well documented with 
the most informative being total annual paddling volume (Figure 4.6). 
Analysis of the multi-year annual training volume reveals a number of salient 
points: 
-- Maximal training volume was attained at age 21 when he trained with the 
USSR national squad.  Annual training volume tended to decrease despite 
periodic deviations in the following years; 
-- Quantitative analysis of the average annual volume over quadrennial cycles 
when he took part in the Olympic Games reveals the following: ages 21-24 
– 100%; ages 25-28 -88.2%; ages 29-32 – 77.4%, and ages 33-36 – 61%; 
-- Analysis of periodic oscillations reveals a remarkable increase in training 
volume in the final years of the Olympic cycles with one exception.  In 
1984, because of political, not methodological circumstances – instead of 
competing in the Los Angeles Olympics that was held in August, the athlete 
competed in a substitute regatta of socialist countries held in July.  As a 
result, the season was cut short by one month; 
-- Reduction of the annual training volume is partly conditioned by longer 
transition periods that increased from one to three months during his career.

It should be emphasized that despite the constant decrease in total workloads, 
Ivan Klementiev continued to have extremely successful performances and after age 
30 won four gold medals at the World Championships and two Olympic silver 
medals. Apparently, workload reduction was effectively compensated for by a higher 
quality of training. This training enhancement was associated with better preparation 
exploiting Block Periodization, a more conscious and effective selection of exercises, 
avoidance of non-compatible workload combinations, constant attention to 
restoration, and the use of a logical program of competition (Klementiev, 1994). This 
great athlete earned a Ph.D. degree, and has been a highly successful coach, serving 
on the national canoe squads of Poland and Spain.  
 
As already stated, long-term preparation is characterized by a cumulative 
training effect, in which physiological evaluations are of special interest. 
Unfortunately, such data for multi-year training among elite athletes are very limited. 


######## IDX 150
139
 
 
Therefore, the case study of legendary cyclist Lance Armstrong is unique and 
extremely interesting (Coyle, 2005). 
 
Case study of physiological changes during long-term preparation. Lance 
Armstrong, world famous cyclist, became World Champion and seven-time Grand 
Champion of the Tour de France, the most famous and prestigious road race in the 
world. From ages 21 to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body 
composition, maximal oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical 
efficiency of pedaling. At age 24 he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and 
during a two year period he came through surgery and treatment that included 
chemotherapy. From ages 27-32 Lance Armstrong was victorious six times in the 
Tour de France, undoubtedly an incredible success in world sport. 
           During a seven year period, starting from age 21, the athlete's body weight 
increased slightly by 0.8 kg while lean body weight increased by 1.1 kg. The 
multi-year trend of physiological variables showed the following (Figure 4.7): 
- 
the maximum oxygen uptake reached peak value at age 23, declined after 
medical treatment and did not reach the highest level until age 28 when he won 
the Tour de France; 
- 
maximum heart rate decreased by 6 beat/min; 
- 
mechanical efficiency, as the ratio of mechanical work to energy expended, 
increased by 8.8%; 
- 
mechanical power obtained at an oxygen uptake of 5.0 l/min displayed a 
substantial increase of 18%. 
It is worth noting that the final estimate of maximum oxygen uptake, 71 
ml/kg/min, is inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 
ml/kg/min (Padilla et al., 2000). It can be speculated that when Lance reduced his 
body weight prior to the races, the real level of maximum oxygen uptake per body 
weight became higher than previously. Nevertheless the study findings indicate 
that the individual progress of this great athlete was determined not by 
enlargement of his physiological potential but by its more efficient utilization. The 
physiological mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency is still unclear. 
The hypothetical contributors to such improvement can be associated with 
pronounced hypertrophy and improved contractility of slow muscle fibers, 
alteration in myosin ATPase activity, increased cycling efficiency induced by 
altitude training and enhanced pedaling technique.

It should be noted that Lance Armstrong attained enormous success after 
extremely serious surgery and medical treatment.  His autobiography is an example of 
magnificent athletic and human fortitude (Armstrong, 2000). Of course, his athletic 
career and individual data are unique. In any case, the tendencies revealed in the study 
of Armstrong’s progress are highly typical. Indeed, many highly qualified athletes 
approach their biological limits but continue to attain their best performances and 
even improve their athletic results. The main source of such individual progress is 
usually better utilization of their motor and physiological capabilities. This improved 
utilization can be conditioned by physiological, biomechanical and psychological 
factors, where individual creativity, self-confidence and athletic wisdom play a great 
role.

4.4 Long-term preparation of young athletes 
 
The athletic career of both world-class and less successful athletes is highly 
dependent on the earlier period of long-term preparation that usually begins in 
childhood. The purview of this chapter restricts consideration of this matter, which is 
worthy of its own book. Nevertheless, the most relevant and generalized aspects of 
young athletes’ long-term preparation will be presented.  This includes the content 
and sequencing of different stages, the concept of sensitive periods in long-term 
preparation, and the basics for identifying gifted youngsters.   
 
4.4.1 Stages and details of long-term preparation 
 
 
The common approach to long-term preparation of athletes assumes that there 
are four separate stages (Table 4.6).

The stage of preliminary preparation varies from one to three years depending 
on sport-specific demands and the age at which the athlete begins systematic training. 
Apparently the favorable ages for starting vary widely in different sports (Figure 4.8).

The common tendency in contemporary sport is a reduction in age for children 
to begin preparation for specific sports. Various reasons explain this trend, such as the 
availability of high quality equipment designed for children (barbells, boats, paddles 
etc.), enhanced training conditions, popularization of sports activities for children by 
the media, and examples of world-known stars who started their sport preparation 
very early. This reduction in the starting age of training and competition has greatly 
affected the international and national sport organizations.  
 
For instance, a few decades ago it was generally agreed that boys should begin 
weightlifting training no younger than age 14. Now the general practice worldwide is 
for schoolboys to take part in international weightlifting competitions at age 11 and 
even earlier. Of course, sport-specific demands strongly affect when newcomers can 
begin and the duration of their preliminary preparation. For example, many juniors 
with previous serious experience in swimming may start systematic triathlon training 


######## IDX 154

early. Thus, the duration of their preliminary preparation depends on how long it will 
take them to acquire cycling and running skills.  This can take about one year. 
Therefore, the data presented in Figure 4.8 reflect worldwide practice but do not 
include special situations in which youngsters begin their training earlier or later.    
 
 
The initial preliminary preparation stage is characterized mainly by all-round 
(multilateral), mostly attractive but not excessive workloads, where harmony between 
basic technical and fitness exercises is of utmost importance (Table 4.7). It is

but in reasonable quantities and using a diversified competitive program. The training 
program as a whole is of great importance for forming and developing proper mental 
abilities that can decisively determine whether long-term preparation will continue.

The third stage of long-term preparation, termed advanced specialization, 
encompasses the period in which athletes attain the real bases of mastery. Usually it 
corresponds to the age at which athletes complete their junior preparation and join the 
adult athletes. Consequently, their technical and physical abilities should approach the 
level of qualified adults (Table 4.9). Concomitantly, training workloads increase 
substantially and may approach those of adult athletes.  
 
It is worth noting that despite increased technical and motor abilities, juniors 
at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads should 
be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic 
exercises requires complete control because highly qualified juniors can be overly 
ambitious in their training routines but not experienced enough in self-regulation of

addition, personal traits such as self-confidence and will power are no less important 
for successful athletic careers than proper techno-tactical and sport-specific motor

brilliant personalities. The individual traits of outstanding athletes have been 
subjected to thorough investigation.

4.4.2 Sensitive periods in the development of different motor abilities  
  
Both researchers and practitioners have remarked that during certain periods in 
an individuals life they are more trainable for certain motor abilities than in other 
times. These time periods have been termed “sensitive periods” and are based on the 
following physiological facts:  
 
a) The natural development of physical (motor) abilities and physiological 
functions in children and youth is non-uniform.  The sensitive periods 
make it possible to make more progress and have the most favorable rate 
of improvement in certain abilities;  
b)  The periods of acceleration and deceleration of motor development for 
different abilities do not coincide chronologically.  Some of them occur 
earlier, others – later. 
  
 
Non-uniformity and chronological heterogeneity in the development of 
various motor abilities are widely known phenomena. However, chronological 
determination of the sensitive periods with regard to specific motor abilities remains 
open to dispute.  Each fitness component can be characterized by various indices, 
which can give different (and at times contradictory) chronological trends. This 
explains the variance in data from different sources. Other approaches entail 
comparing training-induced effects achieved at different ages. Using this approach, 
the sensitive periods were determined and are shown in Figure 4.9. 
 
In general, the sensitive periods are determined by growth, maturation and 
natural trends in the development of the motor system. Physical activity and specially 
organized training are integrative factors that stimulate and augment the natural 
physical trend. For instance, the most favorable period for improvement of general 
motor coordination is between ages 9-12.  Coordinated ability increases at an older 
age as well, but its improvement rate is lower. Similarly, flexibility increases 
considerably more at ages 7-10 when the high elasticity of tendons, ligaments and 
joints is beneficial for making progress. The elementary forms of speed also develop 
non-uniformly.  The highest improvement rate for maximal movement speed occurs 
at ages 11-13 in both girls and boys while reaction time improves most at 9-11 years 
of age.

The influence of growth and maturation is especially pronounced with regard 
to strength abilities. Achievements in the high- and long jump depends on powerful 
muscular contractions and body mass. The latter component increases most noticeably 
in mid-puberty girls aged 13-15; and their maximal improvement rate occurs at 11-13. 
 
Boys perform better in the high- and long jumps at ages 13-17. The 
improvement in maximal strength attained in mid-puberty and late-puberty is directly 
affected by hormonal changes (maturation) and an increase in muscle mass (growth). 
It is well known that improvement in muscle strength is a result of better neural 
regulation as well as muscular hypertrophy. It is worth noting that training-induced 
hypertrophy is much more pronounced in adults in comparison to mid-pubertal or 
late-pubertal children. Therefore, improvement in neural regulation is the main source 
of increased explosive and maximal strength. Improvement in neural adaptation also 
contributes to gains in strength endurance. Other contributors relate to metabolic 
factors (aerobic and anaerobic energy supply) and hormonal aspects. More 
specifically, the androgenic hormones (e.g., testosterone) affect anaerobic power

starts to increase at ages 12-13 in girls, and 13-14 in boys. 
 
Practice has been shown to improve aerobic development greatly in children 
aged 9-12.  However, the most favorable periods for aerobic endurance increases 
appear in mid-pubertal children, from age 14 in girls and 15 in boys. The most 
influential factors affecting this sensitive period are increased body size, and in 
particular, muscle mass, increased heart volume, total blood volume, and a higher 
hemoglobin concentration.  
 
 
The sensitive periods are exploited in training systems with young athletes 
although commensurate pedagogical precautions are necessary. The higher sensitivity 
of children and youth can lead to overload and even injury. This is particularly 
relevant in training for maximum strength and in power exercises.   
  
4.4.3 Identifying gifted athletes 
 
 
In general, giftedness can be characterized as a predisposition to and a higher 
trainability for a given activity.  These are considered to be genetically transmitted 
properties of an individual. In sports, properly developing giftedness implies attaining 
sports excellence. Apparently, the earlier this giftedness is identified, the more 
effectively the individual's athletic preparation can be managed and the greater is the 
probability of developing an elite athlete. Thus, a gifted child is potentially a talented 
athlete and, therefore, identification of giftedness can be based on unchangeable 
inherited predictors of talent.  
 
According to the current approach (Williams & Franks, 1998; Williams & 
Reilly, 2000), sport talent is determined by four generalized factors: anthropometrical, 
physiological, psychological and sociological.  Each of them contains numerous 
characteristics that can serve as predictors of potential talent. Some anthropometrical 
and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as such, can not be 
compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict progress in a given 
sport. Several psychological personality traits are somewhat inherited (Plomin et al., 
1994; Saudino, 1997) and therefore can be altered during preparation. Sociological

conditions are not heredity-dependent.  This doesn’t mean, however, that they can be 
changed easily if necessary (Table 4.11).

The identification of gifted, that is, potentially talented athletes, can be based 
on unchangeable predictors, most often associated with anthropometric and 
physiological factors. This approach led to the development of so-called model 
characteristics, which describe favorable combinations of anthropometric and 
physiological measurements for different age categories (Bulgakova, 1986). The 
characteristics were used for identifying candidates with the best prospects for 
benefiting from more specialized training. The main limitation of this evaluation is in 
the differing levels of maturity of children that are examined to determine giftedness. 
Children with slower rates of maturation may be found inferior to more mature 
teammates but may have greater potential for further progress.

151
 
 
Special attention should be given to determining the most favorable 
combinations of anthropometric and physiological estimates for different ages. Such 
age related models can be created through longitudinal study of a large group of 
athletes, where one sub-group attains the elite level. Data for the athletes recorded in 
the different periods can be used as model characteristics for corresponding age 
categories. It is obvious that such a study, which would take a number of years, 
appears difficult and has organizational problems, but such long-term research 
projects have been conducted (Vorontsov et al. 1999; Falk et al., 2003). Much more 
common are so-called cross-sectional studies that compare less successful and more 
successful youngsters.  The results are used to reveal some specifics about 
hypothetically gifted athletes. 
 
 
Case study and example. 320 swimmers aged 11-18, participated in the USA 
Select Program and were examined with respect to biological age, 
anthropometric status, muscle strength and power, swim-specific abilities and 
performance time. The results showed that the best athletes at younger ages 
are usually more mature than their less successful counterparts while the best 
athletes in the older ages are mostly on-time maturers (80% of the US 
National team) or late maturers (18% of the team). The authors suggest that 
high performing late maturers have better chances of remaining involved with 
the sport for longer periods (Troup et al., 1991)   
 
 
 
Another approach to considering this problem is through retrospective studies, 
in which the development of outstanding athletes is carefully analyzed with respect to 
performance trend, changes in body size etc. The number of available characteristics 
for retrospective analysis is usually limited but the benefits of such studies are 
obvious since this is only way to reconstruct the unique progress of Olympic and 
world champions from childhood to the podium.

Another general approach can be recommended to coaches in any of several 
sports as a part of the initial preparation of youngsters. This approach is based on the 
assumption that giftedness is comprised of two major components, a predisposition to 
a certain sport activity and trainability in related workloads (Figure 4.11).  These 
components determine the effect of initial preparation.  For example, a predisposition 
to a certain sport affects the initial level of relevant motor fitness (speed, endurance, 
agility etc.) while trainability, determines the development improvement rate during 
initial preparation. This assumption has several restrictions since a predisposition to a 
certain sport is not the only determining factor of the motor fitness level that can be 
examined.  Previous experience in this activity (preliminary training, acquaintance 
with tests, etc.) also has a strong effect on the outcome of the initial tests.

One more remark must be made concerning the optimal duration of 
preparation necessary to evaluate improvement rate, i.e., the trainability of young 
athletes. There is no simple unequivocal answer to this question since the following 
circumstances must be considered: 
1) The absolute unsuitability of certain individuals for specific sports can be 
recognized quickly (tall and heavy candidates in gymnastics; small children in 
basketball etc.); 
2) Non-gifted candidates can usually be recognized during short-term 
preliminary preparation lasting about three-four months; 
3) Diagnosing giftedness in maximal speed and power sports needs a relatively 
short period and usually lasts up to one year; 
4) Identification of gifted children in highly coordinated sports (gymnastics, 
figure skating etc.) is limited by the initial preparation, which is usually earlier 
than in other sports (Figure 4.8).  Also, the evaluation process takes between 
1-2 years; 
5) In team and dual sports, where children start systematic preparation relatively 
later (Figure 7.8), very gifted athletes can be identified faster (two-three 
months) but this process usually takes about one year;

6) Perhaps the longest period for giftedness identification is needed in endurance 
sports, where many world-level athletes are recognized as potential elite 
athletes after three-four years of systematic preparation. 
 
Evidence of genetics. Based on the outcomes of studies with young adult twins, 
it has been found that the contribution of heredity related factors to training 
response in an endurance program is different for earlier and later stages of 
preparation. The initial preparation is less dependent on heredity.  However, as 
athletes progress and approach higher workloads, the genetic control of their 
training response becomes much stronger (Bouchard et al., 2000). This 
characteristic of training responses partly explains why some gifted endurance 
athletes cannot be effectively recognized at an earlier stage of their preparation. 
 
A final remark relates to the genetic component of athletic giftedness that 
cannot be underestimated. It relates to a coach's interest in the athletic history of the 
family and the achievements of the older relatives that is both reasonable and 
desirable. Only a few outstanding athletes had great champions among their parents.  
Most of them were born and grew up in families with physically active and sport 
oriented persons.  
 
Summary 
 
Long-term athletic preparation has been considered with respect to designing 
relatively prolonged training cycles (annual and quadrennial), multi-year preparation 
of adult, and multi-year preparation of young athletes. The basics of annual cycle 
construction included goals and objectives, sequencing the main steps in the annual 
plan, and general tendencies in workload compilation. All these items are considered 
in light of the Block Periodization concept.  
 
Special attention was given to seasonal trends in training workloads within the 
annual cycle of preparation (Table 4.3). Particulars regarding quadrennial planning 
were given for preparing highly qualified athletes. Special attention was given to 
workload trends in preparing older and experienced athletes and their younger 
counterparts. Also, the problem of athletic longevity was briefly analyzed with respect 
to the characteristics of the older experienced athletes (Table 4.5).  


######## IDX 168
157
 
 
 
The typical trend in annual training workloads was presented together with a 
case study of many-time world and Olympic canoeing champion Ivan Klementiev 
(Latvia), while physiological changes during long-term preparation were considered 
on the basis of a case study of World Champion and seven-time Tour de France 
champion, Lance Armstrong (USA). It was seen that many older athletes approach 
their biological limits but continue to attain outstanding performances, and even 
improve their athletic results. The source of such individual progress can be attributed 
to better utilization of their motor and physiological capabilities, where individual 
creativity, self-confidence and athletic wisdom play a big role.  
 
 
The common approach to long-term athletic preparation assumes there are 
four separate stages.  They are preliminary preparation, initial specialization,  
advanced specialization, and sports perfection. Each of these is characterized by the 
proper combination of stage length, frequency and duration of workouts, yearly 
training volume and other sport-specific variables. The physical, technical, tactical 
and mental characteristics of each stage were summarized and considered in general 
(Tables 4.7-4.10). 
 
In terms of biological maturation, the concept of sensitive periods is of special 
importance. It assumes there are the periods in an individuals life when they are more 
trainable for certain motor abilities than at other times. Consequently, the periods of 
most favorable training responses can be exploited for more conscientious and 
beneficial development (Figure 4.9). Special attention was given to the identification 
of gifted young athletes, because early identification of giftedness permits more 
effective management of preparation in talented athletes with great potential. 
Prospective and retrospective approaches for determining valid and informative 
indicators of giftedness were considered. For practical purposes and general 
evaluation of giftedness, it is highly recommended that the initial level of sport-
specific fitness characteristics be evaluated as a predisposition to a given sport.  The 
improvement rate of athletic abilities during initial preparation should be evaluated as 
an indicator of trainability. The comprehensive scheme presented in Figure 4.12 
makes it possible to estimate athletic giftedness in general.

Chapter 5 
 
Altitude training 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Altitude training has been a greatly disputed topic in sports science and of 
much interest to researchers and coaches for over three decades. Generally speaking, 
the present situation is paradoxical. Publications written for coaches consider altitude 
training to be an efficacious and proven tool for enhancing high-level performance 
(Fuchs & Reiss, 1990; Dick, 1992; Suslov et al., 1999) while exercise physiology 
textbooks and professional reviews state that altitude training provides no extra 
benefits for sea level performance than conventional training (Jensen & Fisher,1979;  
McArdle et al., 1991; Wilmore & Costill, 1993; Saltin, 1996, inter alia).  
 
From a practical viewpoint, the positive experiences of prominent coaches, 
great athletes and several national teams, offer strong arguments for employing 
altitude training.  Many successful national teams, particularly in the endurance 
sports, incorporate altitude training as part of their preparation. This chapter 
summarizes the current body of physiological and methodological data concerning 
altitude training with respect to training program design. The scientific background 
presented here is limited and readers are advised to refer to other sources (see reviews 
of Boning et al., 1997; Rusko et al., 2004; Wilber, 2004 and others).

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is** — A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works** — **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material: early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
specialization later draws on. The text does not itself restate this mechanism in this
passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25). The text does note one exception: "many Russian
experts" hold that early specialization is possible in sports emphasizing coordination,
agility, flexibility, or speed (e.g. gymnastics), because of the pre-adolescent's
particular ability in those respects; strength and endurance sports are discouraged for
youngsters specifically (printed 25).

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a more granular, sport-by-sport reference
table alongside this library's existing LTAD guidance. It converges with, and adds numeric
detail beyond, the Bompa library's
[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model|Long-Term Sequential Development
Model]], which states a general "not before ~14-15" specialization guideline but does not
break it out by individual sport; this convergence is this entry's own comparison, not
stated in either source.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a 20th-century Soviet sports-school table,
not a modern, population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies
(see [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football, not listed in Table 1.2 at
all) do not map cleanly onto these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as
illustrative, not prescriptive, for a Baylor Athletics context; this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — **Inference:** The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than
early single-sport strength specialization, consistent with existing LTAD guidance already
in this library.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]] (reciprocal link
recommended there: add a line noting Supertraining Table 1.2 gives per-sport numeric ages
that concretize this framework's general specialization-age guidance),
[[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]].
=====

# The Long-Term Sequential Development Model

**What it is** — A pyramid model for an athlete's career: a broad base of **multilateral development** (childhood) → increasing **specialized training** (junior years) → **high performance** (maturity). The proportion of sport-specific work rises as the athlete matures — very small during the multilateral phase, then growing; for advanced athletes, ~60–80% of training time is sport-specific, the rest developing biomotor abilities (the exact ratio varies by sport: ~90% specific in long-distance running, ~40% in high jump). Bompa gives per-sport guideline ages for *starting training*, *starting specialization*, and *reaching peak performance* (e.g. specialization generally not before ~14–15 in most sports; Russian longitudinal data suggested not before age 15).

**Why it works** — Three longitudinal studies (East German 14-year, Russian survey, and a tennis study) found athletes with a strong multilateral base reached higher ultimate performance, with fewer overuse injuries and less burnout, than early specializers — who progressed faster initially but plateaued, lost confidence, and faced more pressure. The base builds the physiological and psychological capacity that specialization later draws on.

**When to apply** — Designing youth/developmental pathways; resisting pressure to specialize a fast-developing young athlete too early; setting sport-appropriate specialization timing; setting the general→specific ratio by training age.

**When NOT to apply** — Some early-entry sports (women's gymnastics, figure skating, diving, swimming) legitimately require young specialization due to early peak ages — the model bends to the sport's maturation demands. The guideline ages are rough, not prescriptive per individual (use [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Deepens [[principle--multilateral-before-specialization]].

**Example** — A talented 12-year-old showing rapid sport-specific progress is deliberately kept on a broad multilateral program, with specialization phased in around 14–15, to protect the long-term performance ceiling rather than chase early wins.
====

# Biological vs Chronological vs Training Age

**What it is** — Three different "ages" govern how much and what kind of training an athlete can tolerate, and they often disagree: **Chronological age** (years lived), **Biological age** (maturational status — best indexed by sexual maturation / circulating testosterone), and **Training age** (years of structured preparation). Prescribe to the limiting one, not to chronological age by default.

**Why it works** — Biological age predicts physical performance potential better than chronological age — more biologically mature athletes are stronger, faster, and better at team sports than same-aged peers. Training age determines readiness for specialization: a high chronological age with a *low* training age still needs multilateral and skill work, not an advanced specialized load. Youth generally tolerate higher *volume* at *moderate* load better than high-intensity/high-load work; combining heavy load with high volume raises musculoskeletal injury risk in the young.

**When to apply** — Grouping and prescribing for youth/developing athletes; spotting the late-maturer being out-competed by early-maturers of the same chronological age; deciding whether an athlete is ready to specialize.

**When NOT to apply** — Don't treat the early-maturer's current dominance as durable talent — biological-age advantages wash out as peers mature. And don't read training age off the calendar; an older athlete new to structured training has a low training age. Pairs with [[principle--individualization]] and [[framework--ltad-sequential-model]].

**Example** — Two 14-year-olds: the early-maturer handles a heavier base, while the late-maturer with the same chronological age is kept on multilateral, moderate-load work rather than being pushed to match — protecting development and reducing injury risk.

- Training residual effects set the retraining cadence: aerobic capacity and max strength both need re-exposure roughly every 30 days; speed needs re-exposure roughly every 5 days or tissue readiness for max-velocity work degrades. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
- The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.16]

## Data, technology and reporting

- The full technology stack: Catapult (GPS), Kitman Labs (central AMS/data store), Perch (camera-based velocity-based training), Polar (heart rate), and the VALD suite — DynaMo, ForceDecks, ForceFrame, Hub, NordBord, SmartSpeed. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Kitman Labs is positioned specifically as the cross-technology data store and analysis/visualization layer, distinct from each vendor's own reporting tool (e.g., VALD Hub, OpenField Cloud). **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7]
- Documented GPS/VALD workflows exist for the full device lifecycle, but Eric's own gap analysis flags them as generic, template-driven, and lacking Baylor-specific detail (serial numbers, storage locations, troubleshooting) except for the Catapult workflow, which has genuine operational depth. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md 3.2.2]
- Credential/login management is currently placeholder-only in the Playbook; a secure credential-vault protocol is named as needed but not yet implemented. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.8; performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 4]
- Standardized weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist; building them is named as unfinished Phase 2 work. **Explicit (gap, stated as a to-do)** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Phase 2]
- Tensiomyography (TMG) is part of the toolkit, with a documented setup/operations SOP, but that SOP is headed with the names of a prior Director and Associate Director of Applied Performance (Althoff, Nelson), not Eric, and current active use is unclear from this corpus. **Inferred (legacy document, status unclear)** [technologytemplatesop.md]

## Education and staff development

- HHPR 5355 ("Power, Speed, Agility, & Periodization in Training") is Eric's own graduate-level course, co-taught with Chris Ruf and Michael Wenger; grading is split across two exams (10% and 20%), a group training-plan project (20%), and lecture/lab participation (40%), with a practical (teach-back) component on exams. **Inferred (transcript, syllabus content)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.1]
- A standalone, 16-week Intern Sport Science Curriculum is proposed, deliberately separate from the Playbook so it can be distributed and revised on its own cycle, aligned to the NSCA Essentials of Sport Science (CPSS) textbook, and adapted from a Clemson model to Baylor's own technology stack (ForceDecks, Catapult, ForceFrame, NordBord, DynaMo, Perch, SmartSpeed, Polar) and to include football alongside Olympic-sport examples. **Explicit** [performance-playbook-development-plan.md Section 5]

Scope: the 11 files in `staging/_scope_issurin_ch4.txt`. Page convention: PDF page = 0-based index = printed + 11 (viewer page = PDF + 1).

**How it was checked.** I rendered every page of the chapter (PDF 136-170) from the source PDF and read every table and figure as a page image: Tables 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, 4.7-4.10, 4.11, and Figures 4.1-4.12. At 160 dpi I also read the figures that carry numbers (4.5, 4.6, 4.7, 4.8, 4.9, 4.10, 4.11, 4.12, 4.1-4.4). I compared the text layer line by line against each entry. I checked three external facts on the web: the Coyle 2005 abstract via the ScienceDaily release, Gore et al. 2008, and the USADA Reasoned Decision. For dedup I checked the vault `Knowledge\library` (Bompa LTAD, Bompa biological-vs-training-age, Supertraining age table, the Issurin Ch1-3 entries). There is no `research-papers` folder in the vault (`Knowledge\` holds career-strategy, coaching-frameworks, faith, frameworks, library, sport-science, tooling). `Knowledge\sport-science` has no hits for Coyle, Bouchard, Troup, LTAD, sensitive period, talent identification or relative age. All `[[links]]` in the 11 entries resolve.

**Global style note (does not drive any verdict).** Every entry uses a suffixed header such as `**When to apply — Inference, mapped to ...** —`. ATOMIZE_BRIEF says "Do not add suffixes." Promoted Issurin entries already carry the same pattern, so fix it here if convenient: use `**When to apply** — **Inference:** ...`.

## Missing (important ideas in PDF 136-170 no entry captures)

1. **Goal setting and failure analysis for the annual plan** (Table 4.1, PDF 137 / p.126): goal, objectives, basic directions and available "hidden reserves", each with a comment. After a failed season the book sets "mutual responsibility of coach and athlete" against blaming external "fatal factors" or the athletes. This is directly usable for season debriefs.
2. **Lower-initial-fitness children may catch up** (PDF 154 / p.143): "children with lower initial fitness levels may possess higher sensitivity to training stimuli and within a given time may equal or even surpass the leaders"; therefore one to two years of preliminary preparation are needed to evaluate predisposition. Competition is recommended "in reasonable quantities". This is the author's own counterweight to the heredity framing and should go in, or be linked from, the talent entry.
3. **Personality traits of Olympic champions** (PDF 157 / p.146): Gould et al. (2002), 10 Olympic champions (confidence, optimism, adaptive perfectionism, sports intelligence, mental toughness, anxiety control, goal setting). Gould & Carson (2007) compare medallists with non-medallists (reacting positively to distractions, performance routines, team cohesion, family support). The book says these matter "also ... in early preparation, although to a lesser extent".
4. **Secular fall in starting ages** (PDF 153-154 / pp.142-143): child-scaled equipment, media and early-starting stars. Weightlifting went from "no younger than 14" to international competition "at 11 and even earlier". Swimmers entering triathlon need about one year of preliminary preparation. This is needed for the Supertraining comparison.
5. **Family athletic history as a genetic cue** (PDF 167 / p.156): coaches' interest in the family's athletic history is "reasonable and desirable". Few champions had champion parents, and most grew up in physically active, sport-oriented families.

I opened every table (4.2 to 4.11) and every figure (4.1 to 4.12) as a page image from the source PDF. I checked three outside facts on the web: the Coyle 2005 result, Gore et al. 2008, and the USADA decision.

**Armstrong case: NO-GO as a standalone entry.** Its physiology is not usable:
- **Opening caveat:** it is unlabelled, uncited, and argues against being labelled. It also claims more than USADA found: USADA disqualified results only from 1 Aug 1998, and the lab tests ran from about 1992 to 1999.
- **Figure 4.7 misread:** it has 5 test ages for heart rate and VO2max and 4 for efficiency and power, not "nine points". The two top-panel lines are clearly labelled, not ambiguous.
- **Text and figure disagree:** the chart puts the VO2max peak at age 22, not the text's 23. It plots power at 5 L/min rising from about 374 to 403 W (about 8%), not the text's "18%".
- **The book misreports Coyle:** Coyle's 18% is power per kg, including a planned 7% weight loss.
- **Published critique:** it is methods-based, not about doping as the entry says: Gore et al., J Appl Physiol 2008;105:1020, "Delta efficiency calculation in Tour de France champion is wrong".
- **Book contradicts itself:** the same page says "seven-time" Tour champion and "six times" at ages 27 to 32.

The report recommends dropping the file and adding a labelled external note to the older-athletes or Klementiev entry. The wording is supplied.
